title: Tutorial 3: Normal models, sampling, and standard errors
text:
Standardising an observation \(x\) from \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) means calculating …
A parameter describes …
An estimator is …
The standard error of \(\bar X\) is …
The CLT describes …







Check your preparation






\(z=(x-\mu)/\sigma\): the number of population SDs between \(x\) and the mean.
A parameter describes a population.
An estimator is a sample-based random rule used to estimate a parameter.
\(\sigma/\sqrt n\), estimated by \(S/\sqrt n\) when \(\sigma\) is unknown.
The distribution of the sample mean across random samples. It is approximately normal for a large independent sample.
crumbs: 11  Tutorial 3: Normal models, sampling, and standard errors

title: Tutorial 3: Normal models, sampling, and standard errors
text:
In the tutorial
Attempt each task before opening its answer. A complete written answer names the quantity, shows the calculation, reports the value and units, interprets it in context, and states one important limit of the model or the data.

Task 1: Population, frame, and claim
A student randomly selects 100 rows from the Shark Tank file and estimates the mean equity offered (equity_offered_pct).

State the population about which this sample directly supports conclusions.
Explain why it does not represent all Shark Tank applicants.
Explain why it does not represent all US entrepreneurs.
State one change needed to target all US entrepreneurs.







Check your answer





The direct finite population is the 1,441 recorded pitches in completed Seasons 1–16. Applicants who were not televised are absent, so the frame does not represent all applicants. The show also selects a specialised group of entrepreneurs, not a probability sample of US entrepreneurs. Targeting all US entrepreneurs would require an appropriate national sampling frame and random selection from that frame.





Task 2: Reproduce the realised sample
The sample is drawn with a visible seed, exactly as in Lecture 7, so every reader gets the same 100 rows:

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
set.seed(123)
sample_rows <- sample(seq_len(nrow(sharks)), size = 100, replace = FALSE)
pitch_sample <- sharks[sample_rows, ]

c(
  n = nrow(pitch_sample),
  mean_equity = mean(pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct),
  sd_equity = sd(pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct),
  q1_equity = unname(quantile(pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct, 0.25)),
  median_equity = median(pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct),
  q3_equity = unname(quantile(pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct, 0.75)),
  deal_proportion = mean(pitch_sample$deal_on_show)
)

              n     mean_equity       sd_equity       q1_equity   median_equity 
     100.000000       12.760000        7.707887        8.000000       10.000000 
      q3_equity deal_proportion 
      17.750000        0.640000 



Identify the parameter, estimator, and estimate for the mean equity offered (equity_offered_pct).
Identify the parameter, estimator, and estimate for the deal proportion (deal_on_show).
Calculate the interquartile range (IQR) of the equity offered in the sample and interpret it. The IQR is defined in Lecture 1.
Explain why a different seed can produce different estimates and a different IQR.







Check your answer





For the equity offered, the parameter is the population mean \(\mu\), the estimator is \(\bar X\), and the estimate is \(\bar x=12.76\)%. For the deal outcome, the parameter is the population proportion \(p\), the estimator is \(\widehat P\), and the estimate is \(\hat p=0.64\). The sample quartiles are \(Q_1=8\) and \(Q_3=17.75\), so \(\operatorname{IQR}=17.75-8=9.75\) percentage points: the middle half of the sampled initial equity offers lies from 8% to 17.75%. A different seed selects a different random set of rows, so all realised sample statistics, including the IQR, can change.





Task 3: Standard errors and sample size
Use the sample output above.

Calculate the estimated standard error of the mean equity offered, \(\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\bar X)\).
Calculate the estimated standard error of the deal proportion, \(\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\widehat P)\) (Lecture 8).
Check the success-failure condition for \(\widehat P\).
Predict how each SE changes if \(n\) increases from 100 to 400 while the estimated spread remains similar.
The sample SD in part 1 was calculated with sd(), which divides by \(n-1\). State that number here and explain it in one sentence.







Check your answer





\[
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\bar X)=7.7079/\sqrt{100}=0.7708.
\]
\[
\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\widehat P)
=\sqrt{0.64(0.36)/100}=0.0480.
\]
The first is about 0.77 percentage points of equity, the second about 4.8 percentage points of the deal rate. The sample contains 64 successes and 36 failures, so both are at least 10. Increasing \(n\) fourfold divides both SEs by \(\sqrt 4=2\). The divisor is \(n-1=99\): the deviations are measured from the estimated sample mean and must sum to zero, so only 99 of them vary freely, and dividing by 99 removes the resulting downward bias (Lecture 7).





Task 4: One pitch versus one mean
Suppose the population mean of the equity offered is \(\mu=13.21\)%, the population SD is \(\sigma=8.44\) percentage points, and samples of \(n=100\) are drawn independently. Supplied values: \(P(Z\le 2.12)=0.983\) and \(P(Z\le 0.21)=0.583\).

State the approximate sampling distribution of \(\bar X\).
Calculate \(P(\bar X>15)\).
A classmate instead models a single pitch as \(X\sim N(13.21, 8.44^2)\) and calculates \(P(X>15)\). Compute that value too, and explain why the two answers are so different.
Which of the two normal models did Lecture 6 reject for the equity offered, and why does the CLT still justify the calculation in part 2?







Check your answer





The CLT gives approximately \(\bar X\mathrel{\dot\sim}N(13.21,\,8.44^2/100)\), with SE \(0.844\). Therefore
\[
P(\bar X>15)
=1-P\!\left(Z\le\frac{15-13.21}{0.844}\right)
=1-P(Z\le2.12)
\approx0.017.
\]
For a single pitch, \(z=(15-13.21)/8.44\approx0.21\), so \(P(X>15)\approx0.42\). The mean of 100 pitches varies ten times less than one pitch (\(\sigma/\sqrt{100}\)), so 15 is an ordinary value for one pitch but an extreme value for a mean of 100. Lecture 6 rejected the normal model for single pitches, because the equity offered is strongly right-skewed. So the model in part 3 is a bad model. The CLT concerns the sample mean. Averaging 100 independent draws gives a nearly normal sampling distribution even from a skewed population, which is why the calculation in part 2 is justified.





Task 5: A proportion through the CLT
The deal proportion (deal_on_show) in the Shark Tank file is \(p=0.612\). A random sample of \(n=100\) pitches is planned, with sample deal proportion \(\widehat P\). Supplied value: \(P(Z\le -2.30)=0.011\).

Calculate \(\operatorname{SE}(\widehat P)\) and check the success-failure condition.
State the approximate sampling distribution of \(\widehat P\).
Approximate the probability that the sample shows a deal rate of at most 50%, that is, \(P(\widehat P\le0.50)\).
Interpret the result in one sentence.







Check your answer





\(\operatorname{SE}(\widehat P)=\sqrt{0.612(0.388)/100}\approx0.0487\). The expected counts are \(np=61.2\) and \(n(1-p)=38.8\), both at least 10. Hence \(\widehat P\mathrel{\dot\sim}N(0.612,\,0.0487^2)\). Standardise:
\[
z=\frac{0.50-0.612}{0.0487}\approx-2.30,
\qquad
P(\widehat P\le0.50)\approx P(Z\le-2.30)\approx0.011.
\]
If the deal proportion in the file is 61.2%, only about 1% of random samples of 100 would show a deal rate at or below 50%. Such a sample would be surprising. Lecture 10 builds the hypothesis test on this idea.

title: Tutorial 3: Normal models, sampling, and standard errors
text:
After class

Timed individual practice: 15 minutes
Do this task alone and against the clock: no notes, no AI, formula sheet only, as in the exam. An invented example: a random sample of 64 customers has mean monthly spending €82 and sample SD €24. Among the 64 customers, 40 renewed their subscription.

Estimate the SE of mean spending.
Estimate the SE of the renewal proportion and check its condition.
State what would happen to both SEs at \(n=256\).
Write one sentence distinguishing sampling uncertainty from selection bias.
Treating \(\mu=82\) and \(\sigma=24\) as the population values, use the CLT to approximate the probability that a new sample of 64 shows a mean above €85. Supplied value: \(P(Z\le 1)=0.841\).
Use \(\sigma=24\) as a planning value. How many customers must a new survey include to estimate mean spending to within €3, at the 95% level (\(z_{0.975}=1.96\))?







Check a model answer





The estimated SE of the mean is \(24/\sqrt{64}=3\) euros. The renewal estimate is \(40/64=0.625\), with estimated SE \(\sqrt{0.625(0.375)/64}\approx0.0605\). The sample has 40 successes and 24 failures, so the success-failure condition holds. Increasing the sample size from 64 to 256 would halve both SEs if the spread remained similar. These SEs describe random sample-to-sample variation, not bias created by an unrepresentative sampling frame. For the new sample, \(\bar X\mathrel{\dot\sim}N(82,3^2)\), so \(z=(85-82)/3=1\) and \(P(\bar X>85)\approx1-P(Z\le1)\approx0.16\). For a margin of €3, \(n\ge(1.96\times24/3)^2=15.68^2\approx245.9\), so the survey needs 246 customers (Lecture 8).





Check your understanding
Complete from memory:

A sampling distribution describes …
The standard error of a mean equals …
The success-failure condition requires …
The CLT says … becomes approximately normal.
A larger sample does not fix …







Check your answers






How a statistic would vary across repeated random samples.
\(\sigma/\sqrt n\) (estimated by \(S/\sqrt n\)).
\(np\ge10\) and \(n(1-p)\ge10\).
The sample mean. For a large sample its sampling distribution is approximately normal. The single observations do not become normal.
Selection bias: how units entered the frame or the sample.






Make it yours (5 minutes)

Utility: two sentences
Think of your EiA venture, or any business you know well. Pick one rate or average you could estimate from about 100 observations (conversion rate, average basket, renewal share), and write two sentences. First state the SE you would roughly expect and what range of sample outcomes would therefore not surprise you. Then say what observed value would surprise you. Lecture 10 turns this idea into a hypothesis test.






See an example, then write your own





Take a student-run campus meal-prep box venture. “From 100 orders, a renewal share near 60% has an SE of about 5 points, so observed shares between roughly 50% and 70% would not surprise me. A share of 45% would surprise me, because it is more than two SEs below what I believe.”



You can discuss this task, and any other task in this tutorial, with Tilly, the course AI assistant: ask it to check the SE you guessed for your own numbers.

Continue to Lecture 9: The t distribution and confidence intervals.

text:
Before class
Total preparation time: about 30 minutes.
Minimum path: the video preparation and the prediction. Full path: everything in this section.
Reactivate (5 minutes). Let \(X\) be the equity offered in a pitch (equity_offered_pct, in percentage points) and define the equity gap
\[
G = X - 15.
\]
Write two-sided hypotheses for the question: “Does the population mean of the equity offered differ from 15 percentage points?”
Predict (5 minutes). Answer the one-click Wooclap question posted on Canvas before you come to class: in a real sample, the unknown population SD \(\sigma\) must be replaced by the sample SD \(S\). Should that substitution make a 95% interval wider, narrower, or leave it unchanged? Commit to an answer. You find the answer in the lecture material.
If intervals, standardisation, or degrees of freedom feel rusty, review Mathematics Refresher: intervals, standardisation, and degrees of freedom.

title: Lecture 9: The t distribution and confidence intervals
text:
Video preparation (20 minutes) Watch Confidence Intervals, Confidence Intervals When the Variance Is Unknown, and Introduction to Hypothesis Testing. Focus on repeated-sampling coverage, the t reference distribution, and the role of the null value. All links are also listed in the External Video Guide.










Check your preparation





Let \(\delta=E[G]=\mu_X-15\). Then
\[
H_0:\delta=0
\qquad\text{versus}\qquad
H_1:\delta\ne0.
\]
This is equivalent to testing \(H_0:\mu_X=15\) against \(H_1:\mu_X\ne15\). Writing the gap as \(\delta\) turns the question into “is the difference zero?”. Regression coefficients are tested in the same way later.
crumbs: 12  Lecture 9: The t distribution and confidence intervals

title: Lecture 9: The t distribution and confidence intervals
text:
Lecture material
Lecture 8 gave a sample mean and its standard error. This section turns those two numbers into a range of plausible values for the parameter, the confidence interval. It ends with the t statistic, which measures how far an estimate lies from a benchmark. Lecture 10 uses it to reach a decision.

Video explanations (review): 20.5 Confidence Intervals, 20.7 Confidence Intervals with Unknown Variance, and Introduction to Hypothesis Testing.


Start with a founder’s question
Suppose an advisor tells you that founders on the show offer about 15% of their company. You have looked at 100 pitches, chosen by chance, and their average equity offered (equity_offered_pct) is 12.76%. Is the advisor wrong? Or is 12.76 simply what 100 pitches can give by chance when the true average is 15? R answers with one command:

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
set.seed(123)
sample_rows <- sample(seq_len(nrow(sharks)), size = 100, replace = FALSE)
pitch_sample <- sharks[sample_rows, ]
t.test(pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct, mu = 15)


    One Sample t-test

data:  pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct
t = -2.9061, df = 99, p-value = 0.004515
alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 15
95 percent confidence interval:
 11.23059 14.28941
sample estimates:
mean of x 
    12.76 


R prints the mean of the sample, 12.76, a t value of \(-2.91\) with 99 degrees of freedom, a p-value of 0.0045, and an interval from 11.23 to 14.29. An AI assistant would hand you the same output with a confident sentence about it. This lecture and the next give you what you need to read the output yourself and to check that sentence: where the interval comes from, why it uses a t value and 99 degrees of freedom, and what the p-value does and does not say. This lecture builds the interval and the t value. Lecture 10 adds the p-value.


From a benchmark to a zero contrast
The driving question compares a population mean to the benchmark 15. As in the preparation exercise, subtract the benchmark and study the gap
\[
G = X - 15,
\qquad
\delta = E[G] = \mu_X - 15.
\]
“Is the mean equity offered different from 15?” becomes “is \(\delta\) different from zero?” A difference of this kind is called a contrast. Every benchmark question can be rewritten as a question about a contrast being zero. Lecture 10 tests a gap between proportions and a regression slope in this way, and names the difference between two groups as a further case.


The price of estimating σ: the t distribution
Lecture 8 gave the standardised sample mean
\[
Z=\frac{\bar X-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n},
\]
which is approximately standard normal by the central limit theorem (CLT). But this \(Z\) contains the population SD \(\sigma\), and in a real study nobody knows \(\sigma\). In practice we replace it by the sample SD \(S\). But \(S\) is itself random. It changes from sample to sample, and in a small sample it can be far from \(\sigma\). A mean that is standardised with an estimated spread therefore varies more than \(Z\). For independent observations from a normal population,
\[
T=\frac{\bar X-\mu}{S/\sqrt n}
\sim t_{n-1}.
\]

Definition
t distribution and degrees of freedom. The t distribution describes a sample mean that is standardised with the sample SD \(S\) in place of \(\sigma\). It is symmetric around zero and has heavier tails than the standard normal. Its shape depends on one number, the degrees of freedom (\(df\)). For one sample mean, \(df=n-1\).

Heavier tails mean that values far from zero are more likely than under the standard normal. The reason is that \(S\) sometimes underestimates the true spread. The degrees of freedom say how much heavier the tails are:

few degrees of freedom mean that \(S\) is an imprecise estimate of \(\sigma\), so the tails are heavier
more degrees of freedom mean more information about spread
as the degrees of freedom increase, the t distribution approaches the standard normal \(N(0,1)\).

For one sample mean, \(df=n-1\). This is the same \(n-1\) as in Lecture 7. Once the sample mean is estimated, the \(n\) deviations must sum to zero, so only \(n-1\) of them vary freely when spread is estimated.


See the R code for this figure
library(ggplot2)

t_grid <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 800)
curve_levels <- c("t, df = 4", "t, df = 10", "standard normal")
reference_curves <- rbind(
  data.frame(x = t_grid, density = dt(t_grid, df = 4),
             curve = curve_levels[1]),
  data.frame(x = t_grid, density = dt(t_grid, df = 10),
             curve = curve_levels[2]),
  data.frame(x = t_grid, density = dnorm(t_grid),
             curve = curve_levels[3])
)
reference_curves$curve <- factor(reference_curves$curve,
                                 levels = curve_levels)
curve_colours <- c("t, df = 4" = "#D55E00",
                   "t, df = 10" = "#0072B2",
                   "standard normal" = "#009E73")

ggplot(reference_curves, aes(x, density,
                             colour = curve, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.3, y = 0.375, label = "t, df = 4",
           colour = "#D55E00", size = 3.4, hjust = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.3, y = 0.335, label = "t, df = 10",
           colour = "#0072B2", size = 3.4, hjust = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.3, y = 0.295, label = "standard normal",
           colour = "#009E73", size = 3.4, hjust = 0) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = curve_colours, guide = "none") +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "dashed", "dotted"),
                        guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.41),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))) +
  labs(x = "Standardised value", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D")
  )








Figure 12.1: The t distribution for 4 and 10 degrees of freedom against the standard normal. All three are symmetric around zero. The t curves put more probability in the tails, most visibly at low degrees of freedom.





The difference in Figure 12.1 is most visible in the tails. The central 95% of the standard normal lies between \(-1.96\) and \(1.96\) (Lecture 6). A t curve must reach further out to enclose its central 95%. The point where the central 95% ends is the 0.975 quantile of the t distribution. It is written \(t_{0.975,\,df}\) and computed in R with qt(0.975, df). This number is called the 95% critical value, or the multiplier. For small \(df\) it is clearly larger than 1.96.






Check: which is larger, \(t_{0.975,11}\) or \(t_{0.975,99}\)?





\(t_{0.975,11}\approx 2.20\) is larger than \(t_{0.975,99}\approx 1.98\). With only 11 degrees of freedom, \(S\) is an imprecise estimate of \(\sigma\), so the t distribution has heavier tails and its 97.5% quantile sits further from zero. At \(df=99\) the critical value is already close to the normal 1.96. With a large sample, the t and normal answers are almost the same. Verify in R: qt(0.975, df = 11) and qt(0.975, df = 99).





The interval recipe
A sample can be used in three ways. A point estimate gives one number for the parameter, such as the sample mean 12.76. An interval estimate gives a range of plausible values. A test answers a yes-or-no question about one value of the parameter. Lectures 7 and 8 gave point estimates. This lecture builds the interval estimate and prepares the test.
A confidence interval combines the estimate with its uncertainty. The general form is
\[
\text{estimate}
\ \pm\
\text{critical value}\times\text{standard error}.
\]

Definition
Confidence interval. A range of plausible values for a parameter, calculated from the sample as estimate \(\pm\) critical value \(\times\) standard error. A 95% confidence interval is built by a method that captures the parameter in about 95% of random samples.


Definition
Margin of error. The part after the \(\pm\) sign: critical value \(\times\) standard error. It is half the width of the confidence interval.

A confidence interval becomes:

wider when the confidence level increases (a larger critical value)
wider when observations are more variable (a larger SE)
narrower when the sample size increases, all else equal.

For an independent sample from a normal population with unknown SD, or approximately for large \(n\),
\[
\bar X\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,\,n-1}\frac{S}{\sqrt n}
\]
is a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for \(\mu\). Here \(\alpha\) is one minus the confidence level. A 95% interval has \(\alpha=0.05\), and the multiplier \(t_{0.975,\,n-1}\) leaves \(\alpha/2=0.025\) in each tail. The words “approximately for large \(n\)” refer to the CLT: for a large independent sample the interval is a reasonable approximation even when the population is not normal. The same recipe applied to the gap variable \(G\) gives an interval for \(\delta\).
The margin of error is the precision of the estimate at the stated confidence level. A smaller margin means a more precise estimate.
This also answers the prediction question from the preparation. Replacing \(\sigma\) with \(S\) makes the interval wider on average, because the t multiplier is larger than 1.96. The extra width is the price of estimating one more quantity from the same data.
In the exam, the multiplier you need is printed in the question or on the formula sheet. For a value of the degrees of freedom that is not on the sheet, use the closest one listed.

Example 12.1 (Worked example: a 95% interval by hand) This is an invented example. A random sample of \(n=64\) ventures reports a mean customer satisfaction score of \(\bar x = 80\) points, with sample SD \(s = 16\) points. The industry benchmark is 75 points. Construct a 95% confidence interval for \(\delta=\mu-75\), step by step.

Estimate. The estimated gap is the sample mean minus the benchmark: \(\widehat\delta = 80 - 75 = 5\).
Standard error. \(\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}=s/\sqrt n = 16/\sqrt{64}\). The square root of 64 is 8, so \(\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}=16/8=2\).
Degrees of freedom and critical value. \(df=n-1=63\), and \(t_{0.975,63}\approx 2.00\). In R it is qt(0.975, df = 63), about 1.998. The closest value on the formula sheet is the one for \(df=60\), which is 2.000.
Margin of error. Critical value times SE: \(2.00\times 2 = 4\).
Interval. Estimate plus and minus the margin: \(5 - 4 = 1\) and \(5 + 4 = 9\), so the 95% interval for \(\delta\) is \((1,\,9)\).

Every plausible value of the gap is positive. The data are consistent with a population mean between 1 and 9 points above the benchmark. Adding 75 back to both endpoints gives the equivalent interval \((76,\,84)\) for \(\mu\) itself. The gap form and the mean form are the same statement.



Check conditions before calculating
The formula is valid only when conditions on the sampling design and on the shape of the data hold. R does not check them for you. Before any interval or test, go through this checklist:

Random selection. Were the rows selected randomly from a defined frame? In the Shark Tank case below they were: the sample of 100 is drawn at random (seed 123) from the 1,441 recorded pitches.
The 10% condition. Sampling without replacement creates weak dependence, but \(100/1441\approx 0.07 < 0.10\), so the usual independent-sample SE is a reasonable approximation.
Shape and sample size. The equity offered (equity_offered_pct) is right-skewed. With \(n=100\) the t approximation for the sample mean is still reasonable. For a very small sample it would not be. Also check for data errors and for single observations that dominate the mean.

These conditions support conclusions about the recorded-pitch frame. They do not make televised pitches representative of all entrepreneurs. The caveat box at the end of this section returns to this point.






Try it: is the average order above break-even?





Try this with your neighbour first. This is an invented example. A venture needs an average order of 20 euros to break even. A random sample of \(n=36\) orders has a mean of 21.50 euros and a standard deviation of 6 euros. Supplied value: \(t_{0.975,\,35}=2.030\).
Step 1 (given). The estimated standard error is \(\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}=6/\sqrt{36}=1\) euro.
Step 2 (you). Calculate the margin of error and the 95% interval.
Step 3 (you). Is 20 euros a plausible value for the mean order? What would you tell the founder?






Check your answer





The margin is \(2.030\times1=2.03\) euros, so the interval runs from 19.47 to 23.53 euros. The break-even value of 20 euros lies inside the interval. The sample mean is above break-even, but the data cannot rule out that the true mean is below it. Advice: collect more orders before any decision that depends on being above break-even. With four times as many orders the margin would be about half as wide.








The Shark Tank case, step by step
Now apply the recipe to the Shark Tank data. The code draws the same random sample of 100 pitches as in Lecture 7 and builds every object step by step:

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
set.seed(123)
sample_rows <- sample(seq_len(nrow(sharks)), size = 100, replace = FALSE)
pitch_sample <- sharks[sample_rows, ]

benchmark <- 15
pitch_sample$equity_gap_pp <-
  pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct - benchmark

gap_bar <- mean(pitch_sample$equity_gap_pp)   # estimated gap
gap_sd  <- sd(pitch_sample$equity_gap_pp)     # sample SD of the gap
n       <- nrow(pitch_sample)
df      <- n - 1
gap_se  <- gap_sd / sqrt(n)                   # standard error

c(
  sample_mean_equity = mean(pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct),
  sample_mean_gap = gap_bar,
  sample_sd_gap = gap_sd,
  standard_error_gap = gap_se,
  degrees_of_freedom = df
)

sample_mean_equity    sample_mean_gap      sample_sd_gap standard_error_gap 
        12.7600000         -2.2400000          7.7078866          0.7707887 
degrees_of_freedom 
        99.0000000 


The estimated population mean gap is \(-2.24\) percentage points. The sample mean of the equity offered, 12.76, lies 2.24 points below the benchmark of 15 points. That is about one seventh of the benchmark. Subtracting the constant 15 changes the mean but not the spread, as the shift rule of Lecture 3 says. So gap_sd equals the sample SD of the equity offered itself, 7.71 points. The standard error is \(7.71/\sqrt{100}=0.77\) points.

critical_t <- qt(0.975, df = df)
gap_ci <- gap_bar + c(-1, 1) * critical_t * gap_se
mean_ci <- benchmark + gap_ci

c(critical_t = critical_t)

critical_t 
  1.984217 

c(gap_lower = gap_ci[1], gap_upper = gap_ci[2])

 gap_lower  gap_upper 
-3.7694119 -0.7105881 

c(mean_lower = mean_ci[1], mean_upper = mean_ci[2])

mean_lower mean_upper 
  11.23059   14.28941 


The critical value is \(t_{0.975,\,99}=1.984\), so the margin of error is \(1.984\times0.77=1.53\) percentage points. The 95% interval for the mean gap is approximately \((-3.77,\,-0.71)\) percentage points. Adding 15 to both endpoints gives the equivalent interval \((11.23,\,14.29)\) for the mean equity offered. The recipe is the same as in the worked example. Only the numbers differ.


Interpret 95% confidence correctly
The parameter is fixed. Interval endpoints vary from sample to sample. “95%” describes the procedure: if the same valid recipe were repeated on many random samples, about 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the parameter.
The simulation in Figure 12.2 repeats the random sample and the interval calculation 100 times. The fixed target is the mean equity offered (equity_offered_pct) among all 1,441 recorded pitches, 13.21 points.


See the R code for this figure
library(ggplot2)

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
set.seed(209)
B_coverage <- 100
n_coverage <- 100
target_mean <- mean(sharks$equity_offered_pct)
ci_lower <- ci_upper <- ci_centre <- numeric(B_coverage)

for (i in seq_len(B_coverage)) {
  repeated_sample <- sample(
    sharks$equity_offered_pct,
    size = n_coverage,
    replace = FALSE
  )
  repeated_mean <- mean(repeated_sample)
  repeated_se <- sd(repeated_sample) / sqrt(n_coverage)
  repeated_critical <- qt(0.975, df = n_coverage - 1)
  ci_centre[i] <- repeated_mean
  ci_lower[i] <- repeated_mean - repeated_critical * repeated_se
  ci_upper[i] <- repeated_mean + repeated_critical * repeated_se
}

intervals <- data.frame(
  lower = ci_lower, centre = ci_centre, upper = ci_upper,
  covers = ifelse(ci_lower <= target_mean & ci_upper >= target_mean,
                  "contains the target mean", "misses the target mean")
)
intervals <- intervals[order(intervals$centre), ]
intervals$position <- seq_len(B_coverage)

ggplot(intervals, aes(y = position, colour = covers)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = lower, xend = upper, yend = position),
               linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(aes(x = centre), size = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = target_mean, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "#C98B2E", linewidth = 0.7) +
  annotate("text", x = target_mean, y = B_coverage + 3.5,
           label = "mu == 13.21", parse = TRUE,
           colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4, hjust = -0.1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("contains the target mean" = "#009E73",
                                 "misses the target mean" = "#D55E00")) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(1, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100)) +
  labs(x = "Mean equity offered (%)",
       y = "Repeated sample (ordered by estimate)",
       colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D"),
    legend.position = "top"
  )








Figure 12.2: One hundred repetitions of the same procedure: draw 100 random pitches, compute a 95% t interval for the mean equity offered. Green intervals contain the fixed target mean (gold dashed line). Orange intervals miss it. In this run, 96 of 100 intervals cover the target.





Each horizontal segment in Figure 12.2 is one 95% confidence interval. Its dot is that sample’s mean. The gold dashed vertical line is the fixed target mean, 13.21. In this run (seed 209), 96 of 100 intervals cross the line. A new run need not give exactly 95, but across many repetitions the proportion approaches 95% when the procedure’s conditions hold.
The following sentence may look natural, but it is wrong:

“There is a 95% probability that the population mean is in my interval.”

Before the sample is drawn, the endpoints of the interval are random, and the 95% applies to them. After the sample is drawn, the interval \((11.23, 14.29)\) consists of two fixed numbers. It either contains the fixed parameter or it does not, and no probability is left. The correct sentence is:

“This interval was produced by a procedure that captures the fixed population mean in about 95% of repeated valid samples.”



From interval to test: the hypotheses and the t statistic
The interval shows every plausible value. A test answers one question about one value: is the gap zero? A test starts from two hypotheses:
\[
H_0:\delta=0
\qquad\text{versus}\qquad
H_1:\delta\ne0.
\]

Definition
Null hypothesis and alternative hypothesis. The null hypothesis \(H_0\) states that the parameter equals the benchmark value, here \(\delta=0\). The alternative hypothesis \(H_1\) states that it does not. A two-sided alternative, \(\delta\ne0\), allows a difference in either direction.

Here the null hypothesis says that the population mean of the equity offered does not differ from the benchmark. State both hypotheses from the research question before you look at the sample estimate. Alternatives that allow only one direction (one-sided alternatives) also exist. They are optional reading in Lecture 10 and are not examined.
The t statistic standardises the estimated gap with its SE. Its general form is the estimate minus the null value, divided by the standard error:
\[
T=
\frac{\widehat\delta-0}
{\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\widehat\delta)}
=
\frac{\bar G}{S_G/\sqrt n}.
\]
First by hand, with the numbers calculated above. The estimate is \(-2.24\) and its SE is \(0.77\), so
\[
t=\frac{-2.24}{0.77}\approx -2.91.
\]
The sign gives the direction: the estimate is below the benchmark. The absolute value gives the distance from zero in standard-error units, here almost three SEs. Now the same calculation in R:

t_value <- gap_bar / gap_se

c(
  estimate = gap_bar,
  standard_error = gap_se,
  t_statistic = t_value,
  degrees_of_freedom = df
)

          estimate     standard_error        t_statistic degrees_of_freedom 
        -2.2400000          0.7707887         -2.9061144         99.0000000 


A t statistic of \(-2.91\) says that the estimate lies almost three standard errors below zero. Lecture 10 measures how surprising such a value would be if the null hypothesis were true. That measure is called the p-value.

What an interval can and cannot tell you

Precision is not importance. An interval that excludes 15 says the gap is measured well, not that 2.24 points matter for a decision.
An interval is not a claim about cause. Nothing here says why offers sit below 15 points.
A narrow interval repairs nothing about selection. It describes the recorded pitches, not founders in general.

What you can do with it: read both ends of the interval as possible truths, and ask whether your decision would be the same at each end.



Answering the driving question
For the recorded-pitch frame, the evidence points to yes. The random sample of 100 pitches gives an estimated gap of \(-2.24\) percentage points with SE \(0.77\). The 95% interval for the mean equity offered is \((11.23, 14.29)\), which excludes 15. The t statistic of \(-2.91\) puts the estimate almost three standard errors below the benchmark. Lecture 10 turns that distance into a p-value and a formal decision. Whether the gap matters commercially, and what caused it, are separate questions that no interval can answer.

A founder’s decision (invented example)
From 25 orders, the average order value is 9.60 euros with a standard deviation of 2 euros. You need 9 euros per order to break even on a kitchen lease. The 95% interval is 9.60 ± 2.064 × 0.40, from 8.77 to 10.43 euros. The break-even value of 9 euros lies inside the interval. The decision: do not sign yet. With 100 orders the standard error falls to 0.20. If the mean stays at 9.60, the interval then runs from 9.20 to 10.00 and excludes 9. You collect orders for three more weeks and decide then.

Next: We can now report an estimate with an interval, and we have measured how far the estimate lies from a benchmark in standard-error units. Lecture 10 turns that distance into a p-value and a decision. It names the two ways a decision can be wrong and shows what makes wrong decisions rarer. It ends with a first look at a regression table, which reports the same five items: estimate, SE, t, p-value, and interval.

title: Lecture 9: The t distribution and confidence intervals
text:
After class
Total practice time: about 70 minutes.
Minimum path (about 35 minutes): read the lecture material, answer the recall questions, then work for 10 minutes on the tasks that follow. Full path: all tasks below.

Read the lecture material (15 minutes)
Read the Lecture material section above from start to end. The lecture covered the core of it. The text has every step, every example, and all the code, including parts that were not shown in class. Note what is still unclear and bring it to the next tutorial, or ask Tilly.


Recall questions (10 minutes)

Why does replacing \(\sigma\) with the sample SD \(S\) require a t rather than a normal reference distribution?
Why does a one-sample t procedure use \(n-1\) degrees of freedom?
What are the three pieces of a confidence interval?
What do \(H_0:\delta=0\) and \(H_1:\delta\ne0\) say?
What does a t statistic of \(-2.91\) tell you?
What is “95%” a property of: the interval you computed or the procedure?







Check your answers






\(S\) is itself estimated and varies from sample to sample. The t distribution’s heavier tails represent that extra uncertainty.
Estimating the sample mean imposes one constraint (deviations sum to zero) before spread is estimated, leaving \(n-1\) freely varying deviations.
Estimate, critical value, and standard error.
The null hypothesis states that the population gap \(\delta\) is zero. The alternative allows a non-zero gap in either direction.
The estimate lies 2.91 standard errors below the null value of zero.
The procedure: about 95% of intervals built this way from repeated valid samples contain the fixed parameter.






Finish a half-worked example (10 minutes)
Re-read the hand-worked interval (Example 12.1). Then complete the same calculation with new invented numbers: a random sample of \(n=25\) customers, mean satisfaction \(\bar x = 42\) points, sample SD \(s = 10\) points, benchmark 40 points, so \(\delta=\mu-40\).
Step 1 (given). The estimated gap is \(42-40=2\), and \(t_{0.975,24}=2.064\).
Step 2 (you). Calculate the SE and the margin of error.
Step 3 (you). Write the 95% interval for \(\delta\) and say whether a gap of zero is among the plausible values.






Check your answer





\(\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}=10/\sqrt{25}=2\). The margin of error is \(2.064\times 2=4.13\). The interval is \(2\pm 4.13=(-2.13,\,6.13)\). Zero lies inside, so a zero gap is among the plausible values, and so are gaps up to about 6 points. The t statistic is \(2/2=1.00\). The estimate lies one standard error from zero.





Practice (10 minutes)
The numbers in tasks 1 to 3 are invented.

A random sample has \(n=49\), \(\bar x=110\), and \(s=14\). Define \(\delta=\mu-100\). Construct a 95% interval for \(\delta\) (use \(t_{0.975,48}\approx 2.01\)).
For the sample of task 1, state \(H_0\) and \(H_1\) for a two-sided test of a zero gap. Calculate the t statistic and its degrees of freedom.
An estimate is 0.42 percentage points per €100,000, with SE 0.18 and \(df=120\). Calculate the t statistic and construct a 95% interval (use \(t_{0.975,120}\approx 1.98\)).
Explain why an interval that excludes zero does not show that a gap is important in practice, or that it has a particular cause.







Check your answers






The estimated gap is \(110-100=10\), its SE is \(14/\sqrt{49}=2\), and the interval is \(10\pm 2.01(2)=(5.98,\,14.02)\).
\(H_0:\delta=0\) against \(H_1:\delta\ne0\). The t statistic is \(t=10/2=5.00\) with \(df=48\), so the estimate lies five standard errors above zero. The interval from task 1 lies entirely above zero. Plausible gaps run from about 6 to 14 points.
\(t=0.42/0.18\approx 2.33\). The 95% interval is \(0.42\pm1.98(0.18)=(0.064,\,0.776)\) percentage points per €100,000, which excludes zero.
An interval that excludes zero says that the estimate is precise enough to tell the gap from zero. Whether the gap is important depends on its size and on the decision. A causal claim needs a suitable study design. A narrow interval gives neither.






Rewrite the wrong sentence (5 minutes)
Rewrite this claim correctly: “There is a 95% chance that the population mean is in my interval \((11.23, 14.29)\).”






Check a model answer





“The interval \((11.23, 14.29)\) was produced by a procedure that captures the fixed population mean in about 95% of repeated valid samples.” The parameter is fixed. It is the interval endpoints that vary across samples, as in Figure 12.2.





Review: one question each from Lectures 8 and 4 (10 minutes)

(Lecture 8.) A planned survey expects a sample SD around 24 with \(n=64\). Estimate the SE of the sample mean, and state what happens to it if \(n\) grows to 256.
(Lecture 4.) From the 2×2 counts table, \(P(D\mid L)=505/734\approx 0.688\) while \(P(L\mid D)=505/882\approx 0.573\). Why are these two numbers different even though both involve the same 505 records?







Check your answers






\(\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}=24/\sqrt{64}=3\). Four times the sample size halves the SE to 1.5. This is the square-root rule.
They condition on different events. The first divides the 505 joint records by the 734 late-season records. The second divides the same 505 by the 882 deal records. Changing the event after the bar changes the denominator.






Check the AI (5 minutes)
You asked an AI assistant: “What does the 95% interval from 11.23 to 14.29 for the mean equity offered mean?” It answered:

“It means that 95% of all pitches offer between 11.23% and 14.29% of the company.”

Find what is wrong and write the corrected answer. This is the Verify step of Attempt → Ask → Verify → Explain, and the exam asks for it.






Check your answer





The interval is about the mean, not about single pitches. In the Shark Tank file, the equity offered (equity_offered_pct) in single pitches ranges from 1% to 100%. The correct reading: the interval was produced by a procedure that captures the mean equity offered in all recorded pitches in about 95% of samples.





Make it yours (5 minutes)

Utility: two sentences
Think of your EiA venture, or any business you know well. Pick one key metric with a published industry benchmark (conversion rate, average order value, churn), frame the comparison as a gap \(\delta = \mu - \text{benchmark}\), and write two sentences: first say what sample you could realistically collect and what a 95% interval for \(\delta\) excluding zero would let you claim, then say what decision would change if the interval turned out to include zero.






See an example, then write your own





Take a student-run campus meal-prep box venture. “The sector churn benchmark is 25% per term. From my roughly 120 subscribers I can estimate \(\delta = \mu - 25\), and a 95% interval sitting entirely below zero would let me claim genuinely stickier customers in my pitch. If the interval included zero, I would stop pitching retention as my edge and lead with margin instead.”



You can discuss this task, and any other task in this chapter, with Tilly, the course AI assistant: ask it to check whether your gap is defined on a population you can actually sample.

Continue to Lecture 10: Testing decisions, errors, power, and the road to regression.
Formula sheet: Lecture 9 formulas.
For a more formal explanation, consult Nieuwenhuis, Statistical Methods for Business and Economics, Chapters 15 and 16.

title: Lecture 10: Testing decisions, errors, power, and the road to regression
text:
Video preparation (15 minutes) Review Introduction to Hypothesis Testing and watch Examples Identifying Type I and Type II Errors. Focus on two-sided tests, decision errors, and why “do not reject” is not “accept.” All links are also listed in the External Video Guide.



Write the two hypotheses of that test.
Say in one sentence what the number \(-2.91\) measures.
Guess: if the true gap were zero, would a t statistic this far from zero be common or rare?







Check your preparation





\(H_0:\delta=0\) against \(H_1:\delta\ne0\), where \(\delta\) is the population mean of the equity offered minus 15. The statistic says that the estimated gap lies 2.91 standard errors below zero. Such a value would be rare: about 95% of a t distribution with 99 degrees of freedom lies within 1.98 of zero. The p-value says exactly how rare. It is the first topic of the lecture material.

title: Lecture 10: Testing decisions, errors, power, and the road to regression
text:
Lecture material

Start with a founder’s question
An advisor said that founders offer 15% of their company on average. Your sample of 100 pitches says 12.76%. Should you tell the advisor that the number is wrong? And what does it cost you if you are the one who is wrong? Lecture 9 ended with a t statistic and no decision. This section adds the p-value and the decision rule. It then gives one workflow for every test and names the two ways a decision can be wrong. It ends with the same test in a regression table, the main object of QM Intermediate.

Video explanations (review): Introduction to Hypothesis Testing and Type I and Type II Errors.



Where Lecture 9 stopped
Lecture 9 compared the mean equity offered (equity_offered_pct) with the benchmark of 15 percentage points, using the random sample of 100 pitches (seed 123). The estimated gap was \(-2.24\) points with standard error \(0.77\), so \(t=-2.91\) with 99 degrees of freedom. The estimate lies almost three standard errors below zero. The open question is how surprising such a value would be if the true gap were zero. The p-value answers it.


A two-sided p-value uses both tails

Definition
p-value. The probability, calculated as if \(H_0\) were true, of a test statistic at least as far from zero as the observed one, in either direction. A small p-value means that the data would be surprising if \(H_0\) were true.

For the equity gap, with \(t_{obs}\) the observed t statistic:
\[
p=P\!\left(|T_{99}|\ge|t_{obs}|\mid H_0\right).
\]
Here \(T_{99}\) is a variable that follows the t distribution with 99 degrees of freedom.
In R, pt() gives the area under a t curve to the left of a value. The two-sided p-value is twice the area to the left of \(-|t_{obs}|\):

t_value <- -2.906   # the t statistic from Lecture 9
df <- 99
p_value <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_value), df = df)
c(t_statistic = t_value, degrees_of_freedom = df, two_sided_p_value = p_value)

       t_statistic degrees_of_freedom  two_sided_p_value 
      -2.906000000       99.000000000        0.004516915 


The p-value is 0.0045. Figure 13.1 shows it as an area.


See the R code for this figure
library(ggplot2)

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
set.seed(123)
sample_rows <- sample(seq_len(nrow(sharks)), size = 100, replace = FALSE)
pitch_sample <- sharks[sample_rows, ]
pitch_sample$equity_gap_pp <- pitch_sample$equity_offered_pct - 15
gap_bar <- mean(pitch_sample$equity_gap_pp)
gap_se <- sd(pitch_sample$equity_gap_pp) / sqrt(nrow(pitch_sample))
df <- nrow(pitch_sample) - 1
t_value <- gap_bar / gap_se

null_curve <- data.frame(x = seq(-4.5, 4.5, length.out = 1200))
null_curve$density <- dt(null_curve$x, df = df)
left_tail <- subset(null_curve, x <= -abs(t_value))
right_tail <- subset(null_curve, x >= abs(t_value))

ggplot(null_curve, aes(x, density)) +
  geom_area(data = left_tail, fill = "#D55E00", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_area(data = right_tail, fill = "#D55E00", alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-abs(t_value), abs(t_value)),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_line(colour = "#17324D", linewidth = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = -abs(t_value), y = 0.33,
           label = "t == -2.91", parse = TRUE,
           colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4, hjust = 1.15) +
  annotate("text", x = abs(t_value), y = 0.33,
           label = "t == +2.91", parse = TRUE,
           colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4, hjust = -0.15) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(x = "t statistic under the null", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D")
  )








Figure 13.1: The t distribution with 99 degrees of freedom under the null hypothesis. Dashed lines mark statistics as far from zero as the observed t = −2.91. The two orange tail areas together are the two-sided p-value, about 0.005.





Read Figure 13.1 with the five-step sequence. (1) Unit and variables: the curve is not data. It is the distribution of the t statistic if the null were true. The horizontal axis is the possible t statistic. (2) Scales: the vertical axis is density, so probability is area. (3) One element: the dashed lines mark \(-2.91\) and \(+2.91\), statistics as far from zero as the one observed. (4) Pattern: the two orange tail areas beyond the dashed lines are tiny, together about 0.0045. If the true mean gap were zero, a sample this far from zero would occur in roughly 5 of every 1,000 samples. (5) Limits: that number is not the probability that \(H_0\) is true, and it is not the size of the gap.
The convention is to reject \(H_0\) when the p-value is at most 0.05. This threshold is called the significance level.

Definition
Significance level \(\alpha\). The threshold for the test decision, fixed before the data are inspected, usually \(\alpha=0.05\). Reject \(H_0\) when \(p\le\alpha\). Do not reject \(H_0\) when \(p>\alpha\).

Here \(p=0.0045<0.05\), so reject \(H_0\). The random sample provides evidence that the mean equity offered in the recorded-pitch frame differs from 15 percentage points. The negative estimate indicates that it is lower.
The same decision can be read from the t statistic. Reject \(H_0\) at the 5% level when \(|t|\) is at least \(t_{0.975,\,df}\), the critical value of Lecture 9. In symbols, \(|t|\ge t_{0.975,\,df}\). That is the same decision as \(p\le0.05\).

c(abs_t = abs(t_value), critical_value = qt(0.975, df = df))

         abs_t critical_value 
      2.906114       1.984217 


Here \(|t|=2.91\) is larger than \(t_{0.975,\,99}=1.984\), so the critical-value rule also rejects \(H_0\).


The confidence interval and test tell the same story
For the same two-sided t procedure:

reject \(H_0:\delta=0\) at level \(\alpha\) exactly when the \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval excludes zero
do not reject when the interval includes zero.

Here the gap interval \((-3.77,\,-0.71)\) from Lecture 9 excludes zero, in line with the rejection. The interval adds information that the p-value does not give. It shows the direction, the plausible size, and the precision of the difference. In this course and in QM Intermediate, always report the estimate and the interval together with the test decision.






Try it: read the decision straight from an interval





Try this with your neighbour first. A colleague reports a 95% confidence interval for a mean gap: \((-1.4,\,3.8)\) percentage points (invented numbers). The report gives no t statistic and no p-value.
Step 1 (given). The two-sided t test rejects \(H_0:\delta=0\) at 5% exactly when the 95% interval excludes zero.
Step 2 (you). Does this interval exclude zero? State the test decision without computing anything.
Step 3 (you). What may you conclude about the population mean gap, and what may you not conclude?






Check your answer





Zero lies inside \((-1.4,\,3.8)\), so the 5% two-sided test does not reject \(H_0:\delta=0\). The data are compatible with a zero gap, and also with gaps as large as 3.8 points in one direction and 1.4 in the other. You may not conclude that the gap is zero. “Do not reject” is not “accept”. The workflow below returns to this difference.








Why zero is the universal benchmark
Many questions about data ask whether a population contrast is zero:

difference from a target: \(\delta=\mu-15\)
difference in probabilities: \(\delta_p=p-0.50\)
difference between two group means: \(\mu_1-\mu_0\)
a regression slope: \(\beta_j\).

In every case, “no difference” or “no linear association” becomes
\[
H_0:\theta=0
\qquad\text{versus}\qquad
H_1:\theta\ne0.
\]
Here \(\theta\) stands for any of the four parameters in the list. A test against a non-zero benchmark can always be rewritten as a test of a contrast equal to zero, as with the gap in Lecture 9. The tests in a regression table have the same structure.


The seven-step testing workflow
Use the same sequence for every test:

Define the population parameter and its units.
State \(H_0\) and the two-sided \(H_1\) before you inspect the result.
Check the conditions on the sample and on the shape of the data.
Calculate the estimate and its SE. For a proportion test, calculate the SE with the null value \(p_0\).
Standardise: \((\text{estimate}-0)/\text{SE}\).
Calculate the two-sided p-value and compare it with the significance level \(\alpha\) that was fixed in advance.
Report the estimate, its uncertainty, the decision, the meaning in context, and the limits.

The significance level \(\alpha\) and the p-value are different things. \(\alpha\) is a rule, fixed in advance. The p-value is a result, calculated from the observed data as if \(H_0\) were true.
If \(p\le\alpha\), reject \(H_0\). If \(p>\alpha\), do not reject \(H_0\), and do not say “accept \(H_0\)”. This answers the prediction question from the preparation: a study with \(p=0.20\) has not shown that the null hypothesis is true. The study may only be too imprecise to tell a real non-zero parameter from zero. The section on power below explains this.

Example 13.1 (Worked example: a proportion test by hand) This is an invented example. An accelerator claims that half of its alumni launch a trading venture within a year. In a random sample of 400 former participants, 232 had launched. Let \(p\) be the launch proportion among all alumni and define \(\delta_p=p-0.50\). Test \(H_0:\delta_p=0\) against \(H_1:\delta_p\ne0\) at 5%, step by step.

Estimate. \(\hat p=232/400=0.58\), so the estimated gap is \(\widehat\delta_p=0.58-0.50=0.08\), eight percentage points.
Conditions under the null. The test uses a normal approximation, so check the success-failure rule of Lecture 8: \(np\ge10\) and \(n(1-p)\ge10\). Lecture 8 gives the reason for the rule. In a test, use the null value \(p_0\): \(np_0=400(0.50)=200\) and \(n(1-p_0)=200\). Both are far above 10, so the normal approximation can be used.
Null SE. Under \(H_0\) the true proportion is 0.50, so \(\operatorname{SE}_0=\sqrt{0.50(0.50)/400}=\sqrt{0.25/400}
=\sqrt{0.000625}=0.025\).
Standardise. \(z=0.08/0.025=3.20\). The observed gap lies 3.2 null standard errors above zero. The statistic is called \(z\) here because it is compared with the standard normal distribution.
p-value and decision. The two-sided p-value is \(2\,P(Z\le-3.20)\approx 0.0014 < 0.05\), so reject \(H_0\). The sample provides strong evidence that the launch proportion among all alumni differs from 50%. The positive estimate places it above 50%.

Report the interval too. A decision alone is not a report. The large-sample 95% interval uses the estimated SE: \(0.58\pm1.96\sqrt{0.58(0.42)/400}=0.58\pm0.048=(0.532,\,0.628)\). It excludes 0.50, in line with the test.
Look again at step 4 of the workflow. The SE was calculated with \(p_0=0.50\), not with \(\hat p\). The test measures how surprising the sample would be if \(H_0\) were true, so the null value supplies the spread.



In R: the Shark Tank deal proportion
Tutorial 4, Task 2 uses the code of this section and the next. Read both sections before the tutorial.
Now apply the same workflow to the random sample of 100 pitches from Lecture 9. Is the proportion of pitches that end with a deal (deal_on_show) in the recorded-pitch frame different from 50%? The code builds every object step by step:

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
set.seed(123)
sample_rows <- sample(seq_len(nrow(sharks)), size = 100, replace = FALSE)
pitch_sample <- sharks[sample_rows, ]

n <- nrow(pitch_sample)
phat <- mean(pitch_sample$deal_on_show)   # sample deal proportion
p0 <- 0.50                                # null value
deal_gap <- phat - p0                     # estimated gap

c(n = n, phat = phat, p0 = p0, deal_gap = deal_gap)

       n     phat       p0 deal_gap 
  100.00     0.64     0.50     0.14 



null_se <- sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0) / n)
z_value <- deal_gap / null_se
two_sided_p <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(z_value))

c(
  null_standard_error = null_se,
  z_statistic = z_value,
  two_sided_p_value = two_sided_p
)

null_standard_error         z_statistic   two_sided_p_value 
        0.050000000         2.800000000         0.005110261 


In the sample, 64 of the 100 pitches end with a deal, so \(\hat p=0.64\). The estimate is \(\widehat\delta_p=0.14\), fourteen percentage points. The null SE is \(\sqrt{0.50(0.50)/100}=0.05\), the statistic is \(z=2.80\), and the two-sided p-value is about 0.005. The success-failure rule holds under the null: \(np_0=50\) and \(n(1-p_0)=50\). Reject the zero-gap null at 5%. The random sample provides evidence that the deal proportion in the recorded-pitch frame differs from 50%, and the positive estimate places it above 50%.


Interval and test: report both
Step 7 of the workflow says a decision alone is not a report. A large-sample 95% interval for the proportion uses the estimated SE:
\[
\hat p\pm1.96
\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}}.
\]

estimated_se <- sqrt(phat * (1 - phat) / n)
proportion_ci <- phat + c(-1, 1) * 1.96 * estimated_se
gap_ci <- proportion_ci - p0

c(proportion_lower = proportion_ci[1],
  proportion_upper = proportion_ci[2])

proportion_lower proportion_upper 
         0.54592          0.73408 

c(gap_lower = gap_ci[1], gap_upper = gap_ci[2])

gap_lower gap_upper 
  0.04592   0.23408 


The proportion interval is approximately \((0.546,\,0.734)\). The equivalent gap interval is \((0.046,\,0.234)\), which excludes zero and agrees with the test decision here.






Optional: estimated versus null standard errors





The test divided by the null SE \(\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}=0.050\). The interval used the estimated SE \(\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}=0.048\). The test asks how surprising the sample would be if \(H_0\) were true, so the null value supplies the spread. The interval does not assume \(H_0\), so the data supply the spread. The two procedures are therefore not exactly the same. When a result lies very close to the 5% boundary, the interval and the test can disagree. An interval that always agrees with the test exists, but it is beyond this course. For the mean gap, the interval of Lecture 9 and the t test of this lecture use the same SE, so there they always agree.





What a p-value is not
The two-sided p-value is the probability
\[
P\!\left(|\text{test statistic}|
\ge|\text{observed statistic}|\mid H_0\right)
\]
and nothing else. The task below gives four sentences that read more into it. All four are wrong.






Try it: correct the four wrong p-value sentences





Try this with your neighbour first. The four sentences are about the launch test of Example 13.1 (\(z=3.20\), \(p\approx 0.0014\)). Each one is wrong. Write a correct version of each sentence.
Sentence 1 (you). “There is only a 0.14% probability that the launch proportion really is 50%.”
Sentence 2 (you). “The result has a 0.14% probability of being due to chance.”
Sentence 3 (you). “Such a tiny p-value shows that the launch proportion is far above 50%.”
Sentence 4 (you). “The tiny p-value proves that the accelerator causes its alumni to launch ventures.”






Check your answers






A p-value is not \(P(H_0\mid\text{data})\). Correct: “If the launch proportion were exactly 50%, a sample gap at least this far from zero in either direction would occur in about 0.14% of random samples.”
The p-value is calculated under the assumption that \(H_0\) is true and chance alone produced the gap. It is the probability of data this extreme under that assumption. It is not the probability that the assumption holds. Correct: “If chance alone were at work, a gap this large would occur in about 0.14% of random samples.”
A p-value measures surprise, not size. The size is the estimate, 8 percentage points, with an interval around it. A tiny p-value can go together with a tiny gap when \(n\) is very large. Correct: “The launch proportion is estimated at 58%, plausibly between 53.2% and 62.8%.”
A significant result says nothing about the cause. The alumni chose to join the accelerator themselves, so they may differ from other founders in many ways. Correct: “The launch proportion among all alumni differs from 50%.”









Type I error, Type II error, and power
A test is a decision rule, and a decision can be wrong in two ways:



Reality
Reject \(H_0\)
Do not reject \(H_0\)




\(H_0\) true
Type I error
Correct decision


\(H_1\) true
Correct decision
Type II error




Definition
Type I error and Type II error. A Type I error is rejecting \(H_0\) when \(H_0\) is true (a false alarm). A Type II error is not rejecting \(H_0\) when \(H_1\) is true (a missed difference).

The significance level is the probability of a Type I error:
\[
P(\text{reject }H_0\mid H_0\text{ true})=\alpha.
\]

Definition
Power. The probability that the test rejects \(H_0\) when \(H_1\) is true: \(\text{power}=P(\text{reject }H_0\mid H_1\text{ true})\). Power is one minus the probability of a Type II error.

Power depends on how far the true parameter lies from zero, so it is always calculated for one given alternative value.
In the launch test of Example 13.1, a Type I error would be to conclude that the launch proportion among all alumni differs from 50% when it is exactly 50%. A Type II error would be to miss a launch proportion that really differs from 50%, for example because the sample was too small.


See the R code for this figure
library(ggplot2)

z_grid <- seq(-4.5, 6.5, length.out = 1600)
critical <- qnorm(0.975)
panel_levels <- c("Null is true", "An alternative value is true")

test_curves <- rbind(
  data.frame(z = z_grid, density = dnorm(z_grid, mean = 0),
             panel = panel_levels[1]),
  data.frame(z = z_grid, density = dnorm(z_grid, mean = 2.5),
             panel = panel_levels[2])
)
test_curves$panel <- factor(test_curves$panel, levels = panel_levels)

rejection <- subset(test_curves, z <= -critical | z >= critical)
rejection$side <- ifelse(rejection$z < 0, "left", "right")

panel_labels <- data.frame(
  z = c(0, 3.6),
  density = c(0.13, 0.14),
  label = c("do not reject", "power"),
  panel = factor(panel_levels[c(1, 2)], levels = panel_levels)
)
alpha_labels <- data.frame(
  z = c(-2.5, 2.5),
  density = c(0.028, 0.028),
  label = c("alpha/2", "alpha/2"),
  panel = factor(panel_levels[c(1, 1)], levels = panel_levels)
)

ggplot(test_curves, aes(z, density)) +
  geom_area(data = rejection, aes(group = side, fill = panel),
            alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-critical, critical), linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "#5B6976", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(colour = panel), linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_text(data = panel_labels, aes(label = label),
            colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4) +
  geom_text(data = alpha_labels, aes(label = label), parse = TRUE,
            colour = "#17324D", size = 3.1) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "fixed") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Null is true" = "#D55E00",
                               "An alternative value is true" = "#009E73"),
                    guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Null is true" = "#17324D",
                                 "An alternative value is true" = "#0072B2"),
                      guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-4, 6)) +
  labs(x = "z statistic", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D"),
    strip.text = element_text(colour = "#17324D", face = "bold")
  )








Figure 13.2: Two-sided testing at α = 0.05. Left: when the null is true, the z statistic follows the dark curve and the orange rejection regions have total probability 0.05, the Type I error rate. Right: when a positive alternative is true, the statistic follows the shifted blue curve. The green area is the power, and the unshaded middle is the Type II error probability. Both panels use the same axes.





In both panels of Figure 13.2, the horizontal axis is the possible z statistic, the vertical axis is density, and probability is area. The dashed vertical lines mark the same two-sided critical values, \(\pm 1.96\). The test rejects \(H_0\) when the statistic falls beyond these lines. This part of the axis is called the rejection region. In the left panel the null is true. The two orange tails have total probability \(\alpha=0.05\), which is the Type I error rate. The test is built to give a false alarm in 5% of samples when \(H_0\) is true. In the right panel one positive alternative value is true, so the curve has shifted to the right. The green area is the power. The probability that remains between the dashed lines is the Type II error rate.
Four changes raise power:

a larger true distance from zero (a difference that is easier to see)
a larger sample (a smaller SE)
less variation in the data (also a smaller SE)
a larger \(\alpha\). This last one has a price. A wider rejection region finds more true differences, but it also raises the Type I error rate.







Optional: one-sided alternatives





This box is not covered in the lecture and is not examined. All tests in this course are two-sided.
A two-sided test asks whether a parameter differs from zero in either direction. A one-sided test asks about one direction only:



Research question
Alternative
Tail that counts




Does the gap differ from zero?
\(H_1:\delta\ne0\)
both tails


Is the gap below zero?
\(H_1:\delta<0\)
left tail


Is the gap above zero?
\(H_1:\delta>0\)
right tail



The t statistic is the same in all three cases. Only the rejection region changes. A one-sided test at \(\alpha=0.05\) puts the whole 5% in one tail, as Figure 13.3 shows.


See the R code for this figure
library(ggplot2)

alpha_tail <- 0.05
tail_df <- 99
tail_grid <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 1400)
critical_two <- qt(c(alpha_tail / 2, 1 - alpha_tail / 2), df = tail_df)
critical_left <- qt(alpha_tail, df = tail_df)
critical_right <- qt(1 - alpha_tail, df = tail_df)

panel_levels <- c("Two-sided", "Left-sided", "Right-sided")
null_curve <- do.call(rbind, lapply(panel_levels, function(p) {
  data.frame(x = tail_grid, density = dt(tail_grid, df = tail_df),
             panel = p)
}))
null_curve$panel <- factor(null_curve$panel, levels = panel_levels)

rejection <- rbind(
  cbind(subset(null_curve, panel == "Two-sided" & x <= critical_two[1]),
        side = "left"),
  cbind(subset(null_curve, panel == "Two-sided" & x >= critical_two[2]),
        side = "right"),
  cbind(subset(null_curve, panel == "Left-sided" & x <= critical_left),
        side = "left"),
  cbind(subset(null_curve, panel == "Right-sided" & x >= critical_right),
        side = "right")
)

critical_lines <- data.frame(
  x = c(critical_two, critical_left, critical_right),
  panel = factor(c("Two-sided", "Two-sided", "Left-sided", "Right-sided"),
                 levels = panel_levels)
)

panel_labels <- data.frame(
  x = c(-2.8, 2.8, -2.8, 2.8, 0, 0, 0),
  density = c(0.035, 0.035, 0.035, 0.035, 0.42, 0.42, 0.42),
  label = c("2.5%", "2.5%", "5%", "5%",
            "H[1] : delta != 0", "H[1] : delta < 0", "H[1] : delta > 0"),
  parse_me = c(FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE),
  panel = factor(c("Two-sided", "Two-sided", "Left-sided", "Right-sided",
                   "Two-sided", "Left-sided", "Right-sided"),
                 levels = panel_levels)
)

ggplot(null_curve, aes(x, density)) +
  geom_area(data = rejection, aes(group = side),
            fill = "#D55E00", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted",
             colour = "grey75", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(data = critical_lines, aes(xintercept = x),
             linetype = "dashed", colour = "#5B6976", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(colour = "#17324D", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(data = subset(panel_labels, !parse_me), aes(label = label),
            colour = "#17324D", size = 2.9) +
  geom_text(data = subset(panel_labels, parse_me), aes(label = label),
            parse = TRUE, colour = "#5B6976", size = 3.1) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel, nrow = 1, scales = "fixed") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-3, 0, 3)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.2, 0.4), limits = c(0, 0.44),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))) +
  labs(x = "t statistic", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D"),
    strip.text = element_text(colour = "#17324D", face = "bold")
  )








Figure 13.3: Rejection regions at α = 0.05 for the two-sided and both one-sided alternatives, on the same null t distribution (df = 99). The two-sided test places 2.5% in each tail. A one-sided test moves the full 5% into the tail named by its alternative, so its critical value is closer to zero in that direction.





A one-sided alternative is legitimate only when the direction follows from the research question and is fixed before the data are inspected. Choosing the tail after seeing the estimate doubles the true Type I error rate, from 5% to about 10%.
The one-sided p-value follows from the two-sided one. When the estimate points in the direction of the alternative, it is half the two-sided p-value. When the estimate points in the other direction, it is one minus that half. For the equity gap, \(t=-2.91\) with \(df=99\):

t_gap <- -2.906   # the t statistic of the equity gap
df_gap <- 99
c(two_sided = 2 * pt(-abs(t_gap), df = df_gap),
  left_sided = pt(t_gap, df = df_gap),
  right_sided = 1 - pt(t_gap, df = df_gap))

  two_sided  left_sided right_sided 
0.004516915 0.002258457 0.997741543 


The two-sided p-value is 0.0045. The left-sided alternative \(H_1:\delta<0\) gives 0.0023, and the right-sided alternative \(H_1:\delta>0\) gives 0.9977.





Preview: the test attached to a regression slope
A regression fits a straight line through a cloud of points. Here the line describes how the equity offered (equity_offered_pct) changes from season to season (season). Its slope says by how much per season on average. R tests every regression coefficient against zero in the way described above. The code fits the line to all 1,441 records of the Shark Tank file:

preview_model <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season, data = sharks)
summary(preview_model)$coefficients

              Estimate Std. Error   t value      Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 20.4565874 0.46442667  44.04697 4.922706e-269
season      -0.8241241 0.04752298 -17.34159  2.514546e-61

confint(preview_model)

                 2.5 %     97.5 %
(Intercept) 19.5455616 21.3676132
season      -0.9173458 -0.7309023


One point before you read the output. In Lectures 7 to 9 we sampled 100 records from the file, so the uncertainty came from the random draw. Here the model uses all 1,441 records. The standard error now answers a different question: how much would the slope vary if the same process produced another set of pitches? The recorded pitches are treated as one possible outcome of that process.
Now read the season row. The slope of the line in the population is written \(\beta_1\), and its estimate is \(\hat\beta_1\).
The estimate is \(\hat\beta_1=-0.824\). Each additional season goes together with about 0.82 percentage points less equity offered. For comparison, the mean equity offered in the file is 13.21 points, so this is about 6% of the mean per season. The SE, 0.048, is the sampling uncertainty of the estimate, in the same units. The t value, \(-17.3\), is the estimate divided by the SE. This is step 5 of the workflow. The p-value in the last column belongs to the two-sided test
\[
H_0:\beta_1=0
\qquad\text{versus}\qquad
H_1:\beta_1\ne0.
\]
The p-value is far below 0.05, so reject \(H_0\). The 95% interval \((-0.92,\,-0.73)\) excludes zero, in line with the rejection.
Every column is something you know from Lectures 9 and 10. The row does not say that a later season causes lower offers. Nobody assigned pitches to seasons, so this is an association over time, not a causal effect.
QM Intermediate starts from this row (estimate, SE, t, p-value, interval). It adds the interpretation of coefficients, models with several predictors, and checks of the model.

What a significant result does and does not establish

Significant is not large. A tiny gap can be significant with a lot of data, and a real gap can be missed with little.
Significant is not causal. The test does not know how the data came about.
No test repairs the data. Selection and measurement stay as they were.

What to report, every time: the estimate with its units, the interval, the decision, whether the size matters for the business question, and the limits of the data.
What you can do with it: weigh the two errors before you decide how much evidence you need.



Answering the driving question
The two wrong decisions are rejecting a true null hypothesis (Type I error, with probability \(\alpha\)) and missing a true difference (Type II error, less likely when power is high). Type II errors become rarer with more data, less variation, and larger true differences. Type I errors become rarer with a smaller \(\alpha\), at the price of more Type II errors. In a regression table, each coefficient row is the test of Lectures 9 and 10: estimate, SE, t, two-sided p-value against zero, and interval.
This completes QM Basic. You can now define events and variables on a frame, describe their distributions, work with conditional probabilities, and model sampling variation. You can turn “our sample mean is 12.76” into a claim about a population, with its uncertainty, its decision, and its limits.

A founder’s decision (invented example)
Your sign-up page converts 10% of visitors. You try a new page on 400 visitors and 52 sign up, which is 13%. The null standard error is 0.015, so z = 0.03/0.015 = 2.0 and the two-sided p-value is about 0.046. Now weigh the two errors. Switching pages for nothing costs you almost nothing, because you can switch back. Missing a page that is really better costs you sign-ups every week. The decision: switch. For a kitchen lease the logic turns around. A false alarm there is expensive and hard to undo, so you would ask for more data and stronger evidence before you sign.

Next: Tutorial 4 practises Lectures 9–10 in exam format. The Mock Exam then covers the whole course under exam conditions. QM Intermediate, in the second year, continues from the regression preview above. The coefficient row that you can already read is the main object of its six lectures on linear regression.
