title: Lecture 4: Multiple regression and what controls do
text:
After class
Total practice time: about 85 minutes.
Minimum path (about 35 minutes): read the lecture material, answer the recall questions, then work for 10 minutes on the tasks that follow. Full path: all tasks below.

Read the lecture material (15 minutes)
Read the Lecture material section above from start to end. The lecture covered the core of it. The text has every step, every example, and all the code, including parts that were not shown in class. Note what is still unclear and bring it to the next tutorial, or ask Tilly.


Recall questions (10 minutes)

Which phrase belongs in every interpretation of a slope from a multiple regression?
Why can a coefficient change after another predictor is added?
What does the no-confounding condition say, and when is it needed?
Why does adding controls not make a coefficient causal?
What problem can strongly overlapping predictors create?
Which five elements belong in the interpretation of a slope?







Check your answers






“Holding the other included predictors fixed.”
The simple slope also picks up the relationship between the outcome and an omitted variable that is related to the predictor. When that variable is added, the slope no longer includes this part.
Nothing outside the model drives both an included predictor and the outcome. It is needed only when a coefficient is read as the effect of changing that predictor.
Unmeasured confounders, selection, reverse causality, and measurement error can all remain after a control is added.
Imprecise and unstable estimates of the single coefficients. With an exact dependence the coefficients cannot be estimated at all.
Estimate and direction, predictor step and unit, outcome unit, the predictors that are held fixed, and the scope (which records, association or effect).






Practice (30 minutes)
Items 1 to 5 practise the core skills. Items 6 to 8 repeat the calculations of Example 21.1 in your own words. Item 9 is the Try it task, now done from start to finish.

Interpret all three slopes from equity_model with units and with the predictors that are held fixed.
Calculate 95% confidence intervals with confint(equity_model).
Test each coefficient against zero. Explain how these three single tests differ from the one overall F-test of the model.
Remove description_words. Compare the coefficients of season and requested amount with those of the full model.
Name one plausible omitted variable and explain which reading of the coefficients it would put in doubt.
Interpret a difference of five seasons with the fitted season coefficient.
Interpret a difference of $500,000 in the requested amount.
Interpret a difference of ten words in description length and use the 95% interval to judge \(H_0:\beta=0\).
Compare two fitted pitches that are the same except that one is three seasons later and requests $200,000 more. Calculate the combined fitted difference.







Check your answers






Holding the other two predictors fixed, among the recorded pitches: one later season is associated with about 0.836 percentage points less equity offered, an additional $1,000 requested with about 0.0029 percentage points less (0.29 per $100,000), and one additional description word with about 0.128 percentage points less.
The season interval is approximately \((-0.936, -0.736)\), the ask_1k interval \((-0.0040, -0.0018)\), and the description interval \((-0.351, 0.095)\).
Each t-test evaluates one \(\beta_j=0\) at a time. The overall F-test (F \(\approx\) 110.6 on 3 and 1437 df) evaluates all three slope coefficients together.
Without description_words, the season coefficient is about \(-0.814\) and the ask_1k coefficient about \(-0.0029\). These are columns (2) and (3) of the table in the lecture material. The coefficients change only slightly. That does not prove that there is no omitted-variable bias.
Examples are the maturity of the venture, its revenue, the experience of the founder, or decisions of the producers about what is broadcast. If such a variable is related to both an included predictor and the equity offered, it is a confounder. The coefficient is then still a correct description, but it is not the effect of the predictor.
Holding requested amount and description length fixed, a pitch five seasons later is fitted to offer about \(5(-0.836)=-4.18\) equity percentage points less.
$500,000 equals 500 units of ask_1k. Holding season and description length fixed, the fitted difference is \(500\times(-0.0029)\approx-1.45\) percentage points.
Ten words go with about \(-1.28\) fitted percentage points, holding season and requested amount fixed. Multiplying the interval by 10 gives approximately \((-3.51, 0.95)\). The interval contains zero, so the two-sided 5% test does not reject a zero coefficient.
The fitted difference is \(3(-0.836)+200(-0.0029)\approx-3.09\) percentage points, holding description length fixed. The two contributions add because the model is additive.






Cumulative mini-task (10 minutes)
Write one paragraph that connects the diagnostics of Lecture 2 to equity_model. Which residual checks would you run on this three-predictor model? What would each check look for? What would you do about a highly influential pitch if you found one?






Check a model answer





A plot of residuals against fitted values checks that the conditional mean is roughly linear in the included terms and that the spread is roughly constant. A curve would put assumption 1 in doubt. A funnel shape would put the usual standard errors in doubt. Standardised residuals (rstandard) flag pitches that the model fits unusually badly. Cook’s distance flags pitches that move the coefficients on their own. A flagged pitch, for example one with an extreme requested amount, is investigated, not deleted: check the recorded values, fit the model with and without it, and report both fits if they disagree. Never delete an observation without reporting it.





Review: one question from Lecture 3 (5 minutes)
For the simple model equity_offered_pct ~ season, the slope’s t statistic is about \(-17.34\). What is the overall F statistic of this one-predictor model, and why?






Check your answer





\(F = t^2 \approx 300.7\). With a single slope, the overall F-test and the two-sided t-test of that slope test the same hypothesis, and F is exactly the square of t. With several predictors this is no longer true. Lecture 5 therefore introduces a test of several coefficients at once.





Worked exam interpretation (5 minutes)
Question. A summary table reports, for the three-predictor model, season  -0.836  (SE 0.051) and description_words  -0.128  (SE 0.114). A student writes: “Season matters and word count does not, so descriptions have no effect on equity.” Give two corrections, in the style of Question 4 of the mock exam.






Check a model answer





First, “no effect” misreads a result that is not significant. The interval \((-0.351, 0.095)\) contains zero and also values near \(-0.35\). The data fit no association and they also fit a small negative one. Not significant does not mean zero. Second, “effect” claims causation. Both estimates are associations among the recorded pitches, holding the other included predictors fixed. The data do not come from an experiment, so they do not show a causal effect.





Check the AI (5 minutes)
You asked an AI assistant: “I added the requested amount as a control. Is the season coefficient of -0.81 now the effect of time?” It answered:

“Yes. Because you controlled for the requested amount, one later season now causes 0.81 percentage points less equity.”

Find what is wrong and write the corrected answer. This is the Verify step of Attempt → Ask → Verify → Explain, and the exam asks for it.






Check your answer





A control only holds fixed what was measured and included. Venture maturity, founder experience, and the choices of the producers are not in the model. The correct sentence: at the same requested amount, one later season is associated with about 0.81 percentage points less equity offered.





Make it yours (5 minutes)

Utility: two sentences
Think of your EiA3 venture, or any business you know well. Name one outcome you care about and two of its drivers that are correlated with each other (for example price and quality tier, or marketing spend and firm age). Then write two sentences. Which comparison would a regression of the outcome on only one driver mix together? What would “holding the other fixed” let you see? There is no wrong answer.






See an example, then write your own





Take a student-run venture that sells meal-prep boxes on campus (an invented example). “Outcome: weekly orders. Drivers: price and quality tier, which move together because premium boxes cost more. A regression of orders on price alone would mix cheaper boxes with lower-tier boxes. Holding the tier fixed shows what a price cut does within a tier, and that is the number I can act on.”



You can discuss this task, and any other task in this chapter, with Tilly, the course AI assistant. Ask it to propose an omitted variable for the regression of your venture, and to ask you whether a measured control could fix it.

Continue to Lecture 5: Categories as predictors and joint tests.
Code sheet: Lecture 4 commands and formulas.
For a more formal treatment, see James et al., An Introduction to Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., Sections 3.2 and 3.3.3, and Nieuwenhuis, Statistical Methods for Business and Economics, Chapter 20.

Before class

Minimum path: the video and the R task. Full path: everything in this section.
Bring a charged laptop with RStudio and the course project open. The code of the lecture is in this chapter, ready to copy, so you can run each step yourself during the lecture and get the same numbers and figures.
Reactivate and predict (5 minutes). The Shark Tank file sorts the presenting teams into three categories: all_men, all_women, and mixed. The video explains dummy variables, which take only the values 0 and 1. How many dummy variables does a model with an intercept need for three categories? Write down a number. Then answer the one-click Wooclap question posted on Canvas before you come to class: at the same season and requested amount, do you expect all-women teams to offer more, less, or about the same equity as all-men teams? You find both answers in the lecture material.
R warm-up (10 minutes). The lecture material starts from the subset and the factor that you build here. Run the code and bring the contrasts table that it prints:
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
known_gender <- subset(sharks, pitcher_gender_group != "unknown")
known_gender$gender <- relevel(factor(known_gender$pitcher_gender_group),
                               ref = "all_men")
known_gender$ask_1k <- known_gender$ask_amount_usd / 1000
levels(known_gender$gender)
contrasts(known_gender$gender)
If indicators and reference categories are unfamiliar, review Mathematics Refresher: indicators and reference categories.

Focus on predictors that are categories (the video calls them qualitative predictors) and on how the reference category decides what a coefficient means. All links are also listed in the External Video Guide.

title: Lecture 5: Categories as predictors and joint tests
text:
Lecture material
This section first compares the groups of teams with plain averages. It then shows how a variable made of categories enters a regression, and how to test several coefficients at once.

Start with a founder’s question
Founders compare groups all the time: customers from the app against customers from the website, one price against another, one kind of team against another. Start with the comparison in the driving question. The Shark Tank file sorts the presenting teams into all men, all women, and mixed (pitcher_gender_group). What equity (equity_offered_pct) did each group offer on average?

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
known <- subset(sharks, pitcher_gender_group != "unknown")
round(tapply(known$equity_offered_pct, known$pitcher_gender_group, mean), 2)

  all_men all_women     mixed 
    13.20     14.02     12.17 

table(known$pitcher_gender_group)


  all_men all_women     mixed 
      773       385       276 


All-men teams offered 13.20% on average, all-women teams 14.02%, and mixed teams 12.17%. The gap between all-women and all-men teams is 0.82 percentage points, about 6% of the all-men average. Three questions follow. Is this gap more than chance? Does it remain when we compare teams from the same season that asked for the same amount? And how does a variable made of words, not numbers, get into lm() at all? The sections below answer them in reverse order.


Measurement first: what the category records

Stanford explanation (review): 3.5 Extensions of the Linear Model.

The categories describe the people who presented on screen: all men, all women, or mixed. They do not record the share of women in a team, and they do not describe the full team behind the venture. Seven records are classified as unknown. They are left out of every model in this lecture. The section on the unknown records further down explains why. Keep these limits in mind for every result in this chapter.


A two-level indicator

Definition
Dummy variable. A variable that takes only the values 0 and 1. It is 1 when an observation belongs to a category and 0 when it does not. Another name is indicator.
Reference category. The category for which all dummies are 0. Every dummy coefficient is a comparison with this category. Another name is reference group.

For a dummy variable \(D_i\in\{0,1\}\),
\[
E[Y_i\mid D_i]=\beta_0+\beta_1D_i.
\]
Then
\[
E[Y_i\mid D_i=0]=\beta_0,
\qquad
E[Y_i\mid D_i=1]=\beta_0+\beta_1.
\]
So \(\beta_1\) is the expected difference between the group with \(D=1\) and the reference group with \(D=0\). A regression on one dummy is the same thing as a comparison of two group means.
This is also how an A/B test is analysed. In an A/B test you show two versions of a page, a price, or an offer to customers, and chance decides who sees which version. Code the version as a dummy and read its coefficient. Because chance decided who saw which version, nothing else differs between the two groups on average. In that case, and only in that case, the coefficient can be read as the effect of the change.

Example 22.1 (Worked example: two group means from two coefficients) Restrict to the all-men and all-women teams (1,158 records) and let women_team equal 1 for all-women teams:

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
known_gender <- subset(sharks, pitcher_gender_group != "unknown")
two_groups <- subset(known_gender,
                     pitcher_gender_group %in% c("all_men", "all_women"))
two_groups$women_team <- as.integer(
  two_groups$pitcher_gender_group == "all_women"
)
coef(lm(equity_offered_pct ~ women_team, data = two_groups))

(Intercept)  women_team 
 13.1973739   0.8210677 

tapply(two_groups$equity_offered_pct, two_groups$women_team, mean)

       0        1 
13.19737 14.01844 


Read the two coefficients as two marks on the equity axis (Figure 22.1). The intercept \(\hat\beta_0\approx 13.20\) is the mean of the all-men teams. The sum \(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1\approx 13.20+0.82=14.02\) is the mean of the all-women teams. The coefficient \(\hat\beta_1\approx 0.82\) is the gap between the two marks.



See the drawing code (optional, not exam material)
old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mar = c(3.5, 1, 1, 1))
plot(NA, xlim = c(12.6, 14.6), ylim = c(0, 1), axes = FALSE,
     xlab = "", ylab = "")
axis(1, at = seq(12.6, 14.6, by = 0.4))
mtext("Mean initial equity offered (%)", side = 1, line = 2.4, cex = 0.9)
segments(13.20, 0.15, 13.20, 0.55, col = "#0072B2", lwd = 4)
segments(14.02, 0.15, 14.02, 0.55, col = "#D55E00", lwd = 4)
arrows(13.20, 0.38, 14.02, 0.38, length = 0.08, code = 3, col = "#17324D")
text(13.20, 0.72, expression(hat(beta)[0] == 13.20), col = "#0072B2")
text(14.02, 0.72, expression(hat(beta)[0] + hat(beta)[1] == 14.02), col = "#D55E00")
text(13.61, 0.25, expression(hat(beta)[1] == 0.82), col = "#17324D", cex = 0.9)
par(old_par)








Figure 22.1: The model with one dummy places the two group means as two marks on the axis of the equity offered. The intercept is the mean of the reference group (all-men teams), and the dummy coefficient is the distance between the marks.







More than two categories
With \(G\) categories and an intercept, use \(G-1\) dummies. With all \(G\) dummies and an intercept, the dummies sum to 1 in every row. This is the exact linear dependence from Lecture 4, and the coefficients cannot be estimated. The mistake is called the dummy-variable trap.
R creates the dummies itself when a predictor is a factor. Choose the reference category yourself and check it. This is the code of the R warm-up:

known_gender$gender <- relevel(factor(known_gender$pitcher_gender_group),
                               ref = "all_men")
known_gender$ask_1k <- known_gender$ask_amount_usd / 1000
levels(known_gender$gender)

[1] "all_men"   "all_women" "mixed"    

contrasts(known_gender$gender)

          all_women mixed
all_men           0     0
all_women         1     0
mixed             0     1


Each row of the contrasts table is a category. Each column is one dummy. The reference category all_men is the row with only zeros. Its mean is carried by the intercept. This answers the first question from before class: three categories need two dummies.






Check: four industries and an intercept, how many dummies?





Three. One industry is the reference group, carried by the intercept. Each of the three dummy coefficients compares one of the other industries with it. Four dummies and an intercept would be the dummy-variable trap.









Try it: three sales channels





Try this with your neighbour first. In an invented example, a venture sells through three channels: the campus stand, the app, and the website. A model of the order value in euros uses the campus stand as the reference and reports channelApp 6.0 and channelWebsite 2.5, with an intercept of 9.0.
Step 1 (given). With three categories and an intercept, the model needs two dummies. The campus stand has no dummy. Its mean is the intercept.
Step 2 (you). Give the fitted mean order value for each of the three channels.
Step 3 (you). By how much does the fitted order value in the app differ from the website? Neither is the reference group.






Check your answer





Campus stand: 9.0 euros. App: 9.0 + 6.0 = 15.0 euros. Website: 9.0 + 2.5 = 11.5 euros. App minus website: 6.0 - 2.5 = 3.5 euros. Two coefficients that share a reference group can be subtracted from each other.








Percent versus percentage points
One point about units comes first. The outcome equity_offered_pct is measured in percent, so its regression coefficients are in percentage points. The next section estimates a coefficient of 1.28 for all-women teams. The sentence “the all-women coefficient is 1.28%” would be ambiguous. It could mean:

a relative change: 1.28% of the all-men level more (13.0% would become about 13.2%)
an absolute change of 1.28 percentage points (13.0% would become 14.28%).

The two readings differ by a factor of about eight here. A coefficient for an outcome in percent is always the absolute kind. The precise sentence is: “At the same season and requested amount, all-women presenting teams are fitted to offer 1.28 equity percentage points more than all-men presenting teams.” Always write percentage points for this outcome.


The adjusted comparison
Now fit the model of the driving question. It contains both category dummies, and it holds season and requested amount (in thousands of dollars, ask_1k) fixed.

gender_model <- lm(
  equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + gender,
  data = known_gender
)
summary(gender_model)


Call:
lm(formula = equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + gender, data = known_gender)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-16.118  -4.778  -1.100   3.220  82.590 

Coefficients:
                  Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)     20.8388333  0.5064929  41.143  < 2e-16 ***
season          -0.8238940  0.0477959 -17.238  < 2e-16 ***
ask_1k          -0.0026613  0.0005822  -4.571 5.28e-06 ***
genderall_women  1.2835231  0.4810241   2.668  0.00771 ** 
gendermixed      0.1209343  0.5411539   0.223  0.82320    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 7.612 on 1429 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.1913,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.189 
F-statistic: 84.49 on 4 and 1429 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Interpret both dummy coefficients with a full sentence. Each sentence names the two categories, the unit, the predictors that are held fixed, and the records it is about:

All-women versus all-men. Among the 1,434 pitches with a known team classification, all-women presenting teams are fitted to offer about 1.28 equity percentage points more than all-men presenting teams at the same season and requested amount (p \(\approx\) 0.008).
Mixed versus all-men. Among the same pitches, mixed teams are fitted to offer about 0.12 percentage points more than all-men teams at the same season and requested amount (p \(\approx\) 0.823). This estimate is not statistically distinguishable from zero.

The first sentence answers the Wooclap question from before class: all-women teams offer more. The adjusted gap between all-women and all-men teams (1.28 points) is larger than the raw gap from the worked example (0.82 points). Holding season and requested amount fixed changed the comparison. This is why the sentence must name what is held fixed. Both coefficients are comparisons with the reference group. They do not show that the gender of a team causes the offer.
Changing the reference group changes the names and values of the coefficients. It does not change the fitted values or the overall fit. Check it:

known_gender$gender_women_ref <- relevel(known_gender$gender,
                                         ref = "all_women")
coef(lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + gender_women_ref,
        data = known_gender))

            (Intercept)                  season                  ask_1k 
           22.122356419            -0.823893957            -0.002661283 
gender_women_refall_men   gender_women_refmixed 
           -1.283523102            -1.162588850 


The same three fitted group means are now described as comparisons with the all-women teams. The all-men coefficient is \(-1.28\), the same gap as before with the opposite sign, and the fitted values are identical.


Are the category terms worth having at all?
So far the coefficients were read one at a time. The driving question also asks something that no single t-test answers: do the two category terms together add information beyond season and requested amount?

Definition
Partial F-test. A test of whether several coefficients are all zero at the same time. It compares a complete model with a reduced model that leaves out the tested terms. Both models are fitted on the same observations.

Two such models are called nested: the reduced model is the complete model with the tested coefficients set to zero. Figure 22.2 shows the pair for the two category dummies.


See the drawing code (optional, not exam material)
old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mar = c(0.3, 0.3, 0.3, 0.3))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 5), axes = FALSE,
     xlab = "", ylab = "", xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
rect(0.4, 1.1, 4.6, 3.9, col = "#DCEAF3", border = "#17324D", lwd = 2)
rect(5.4, 1.1, 9.6, 3.9, col = "#FDE5C1", border = "#17324D", lwd = 2)
text(2.5, 3.35, "Reduced model", font = 2, col = "#17324D")
text(2.5, 2.55, "season + ask_1k", cex = 0.95)
text(2.5, 1.85, expression(beta[aw] == 0 ~ "," ~ beta[mx] == 0),
     cex = 0.95, col = "#5B6976")
text(7.5, 3.35, "Complete model", font = 2, col = "#17324D")
text(7.5, 2.55, "season + ask_1k", cex = 0.95)
text(7.5, 1.85, "+ two category dummies", cex = 0.95)
arrows(4.7, 2.5, 5.3, 2.5, length = 0.1, lwd = 2, col = "#17324D")
text(5.0, 3.0, "free the\ntwo coefficients", cex = 0.8, col = "#5B6976")
par(old_par)








Figure 22.2: The two nested models of the partial F-test. The reduced model is the complete model with the two category coefficients set to zero, fitted on the same observations.





The hypotheses:
\[
H_0:\beta_{all\_women}=\beta_{mixed}=0
\quad\text{against at least one non-zero.}
\]

Example 22.2 (Worked example: the partial F statistic by hand) Fit both models and ask R for the anova table:

reduced_gender <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k,
                     data = known_gender)
anova(reduced_gender, gender_model)

Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k
Model 2: equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + gender
  Res.Df   RSS Df Sum of Sq      F Pr(>F)  
1   1431 83228                             
2   1429 82792  2    436.25 3.7649 0.0234 *
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Now calculate F by hand from the numbers in the table. The residual sum of squares (RSS in the R output, SSE in this course) falls by \(436.25\) when the two category terms are added. This uses \(2\) degrees of freedom. The complete model leaves a residual sum of squares of \(82{,}792\) on \(1{,}429\) degrees of freedom:
\[
F=\frac{436.25/2}{82{,}792/1{,}429}
=\frac{218.13}{57.94}
\approx 3.76.
\]
Read the ratio. The numerator is the variation that the two terms explain, per tested coefficient. The denominator is the variation that is left unexplained, per residual degree of freedom. If the two coefficients were really zero, the ratio would be close to 1. Here it is about 3.8, and the p-value is about 0.023.

At 5%, the two category terms are jointly useful in this model. Compare this with the single results: the p-value of the joint test is \(0.023\), and the p-value of the mixed dummy alone is \(0.823\). Joint usefulness is not the same as individual significance. The F-test asks whether the two terms together improve the model. It does not ask whether each term is significant on its own. The overall F-test in summary(gender_model), about 84.5 with a very small p-value, answers a third question: whether all four coefficients together improve on a model with only an intercept.


Visualise the adjusted comparison
Figure 22.3 shows the fitted equity offered for the three groups of teams at the same season and requested amount.


See the R code for this figure
library(ggplot2)
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
known_gender <- subset(sharks, pitcher_gender_group != "unknown")
known_gender$gender <- relevel(factor(known_gender$pitcher_gender_group),
                               ref = "all_men")
known_gender$ask_1k <- known_gender$ask_amount_usd / 1000
gender_model <- lm(
  equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + gender,
  data = known_gender
)
newdat <- data.frame(
  season = mean(known_gender$season),
  ask_1k = mean(known_gender$ask_1k),
  gender = factor(c("all_men", "all_women", "mixed"),
                  levels = levels(known_gender$gender))
)
pred <- predict(gender_model, newdata = newdat, interval = "confidence")
adj_df <- data.frame(
  team = factor(c("All-men", "All-women", "Mixed"),
                levels = c("All-men", "All-women", "Mixed")),
  fit = pred[, "fit"],
  lwr = pred[, "lwr"],
  upr = pred[, "upr"]
)

ggplot(adj_df, aes(x = team, y = fit)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr),
                  colour = "#009E73", linewidth = 0.7, fatten = 2.6) +
  labs(x = "Source classification of pitching team",
       y = "Fitted initial equity offered (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D")
  )








Figure 22.3: Fitted equity offered for the three groups of presenting teams at the average season and requested amount, with 95% confidence intervals. The all-women point lies above the other two. The intervals show sampling uncertainty under the model, not uncertainty about how the categories were recorded.





Read Figure 22.3 with the five steps for reading a figure:

Unit and variables: the horizontal axis shows the three categories of teams. The vertical axis shows the fitted equity offered, in percent.
Scales: each point is a fitted mean at the same average season and requested amount. This is an adjusted comparison, not a comparison of raw group means.
One element: the points are fitted values (about 12.9, 14.1, and 13.0). The vertical lines are 95% confidence intervals. They are wider for the smaller groups.
Pattern: the all-women point lies about 1.28 points above the all-men point. The mixed interval overlaps both.
Limits: the intervals show sampling uncertainty under the model. They say nothing about how well the broad categories were recorded, and nothing about causes.



Why unknown is excluded, not a fourth group
Seven records have the classification unknown. This label says that information is missing. It is not a kind of team. A fourth category would estimate the mean equity of teams that the source could not classify, a number with no business meaning. Leaving these records out keeps every coefficient interpretable. The cost is that the results describe the 1,434 classified records only.

What these category coefficients can and cannot say

The categories are a broad description of the people who presented. They do not record shares of women, and they do not describe the full founding team.
Each coefficient compares one group with the reference group, at the same season and requested amount.
The model says that offers differ between the coded groups. It does not say that the composition of a team makes anyone offer differently.

What you can do with it: for groups that you can assign yourself, such as two versions of a page, run an A/B test. Then the group coefficient is the effect.



Answering the driving question
At the same season and requested amount, all-women presenting teams are fitted to offer about 1.28 equity percentage points more than all-men teams (p \(\approx\) 0.008). That is about one tenth of the average equity offered by all-men teams (13.20%). Mixed teams cannot be distinguished from all-men teams. The two category terms are jointly useful (partial F \(\approx\) 3.76, p \(\approx\) 0.023), so they belong in the model. The result is an adjusted association among these recorded pitches, not an effect of gender.

A founder’s decision (invented example)
You test two checkout pages. Each new customer sees the old or the new page by chance, 100 customers each. You regress the order value in euros on a dummy for the new page. The coefficient is 1.20 with a standard error of 0.50, so the 95% interval runs from about 0.20 to 2.20 euros. Chance decided who saw which page, so the two groups differ in nothing else on average. Here the coefficient is the effect of the page. The decision: switch to the new page. This is an A/B test, the founder’s own way to get from an association to an effect.

Next: You can now compare categories at fixed values of the other predictors. So far every group has the same slope, and every trend is a straight line. Both are choices of the model, not facts. Lecture 6 relaxes them. An interaction lets the season trend differ between groups of teams, and a squared term lets the trend bend.

title: Lecture 5: Categories as predictors and joint tests
text:
After class
Total practice time: about 80 minutes.
Minimum path (about 35 minutes): read the lecture material, answer the recall questions, then work for 10 minutes on the tasks that follow. Full path: all tasks below.

Read the lecture material (15 minutes)
Read the Lecture material section above from start to end. The lecture covered the core of it. The text has every step, every example, and all the code, including parts that were not shown in class. Note what is still unclear and bring it to the next tutorial, or ask Tilly.


Recall questions (10 minutes)

Why are only \(G-1\) dummies used with an intercept?
What does a dummy coefficient compare?
What changes when the reference group changes?
What does a partial F-test evaluate?
Why can a joint F-test reject when one individual t-test does not?
How is an A/B test analysed with a regression, and why can its coefficient be read as an effect?







Check your answers






All \(G\) dummies sum to 1 in every row, which is the same as the intercept column. This is an exact linear dependence, so the coefficients could not be estimated.
A category with the named reference category, holding the other included predictors fixed.
The names and values of the coefficients change, because they now compare with a different category. The fitted values and the overall fit do not change.
Whether several coefficients are all zero at the same time. It compares two nested models on the same observations.
The F-test evaluates the terms together. Each t-test asks a narrower question about one comparison with the reference group, and it can miss what the terms explain together.
Code the version (A or B) as a dummy and regress the outcome on it. The coefficient is the difference between the two group means. Chance decided who saw which version, so the groups differ in nothing else on average, and the difference is the effect of the version.






Releveling and verification practice (15 minutes)

Relevel gender so that mixed is the reference group, and interpret both dummy coefficients. Save the relevelled model as relevelled_model.
Check that the fitted values are unchanged after releveling by comparing them with those of gender_model.
State the hypotheses for the partial F-test of both gender dummies.
Explain why the seven unknown records were left out and not treated as a fourth group.
Explain why “the all-women coefficient is 1.28%” is ambiguous, then rewrite it precisely.







Check your answers






Use:
mixed_reference <- relevel(known_gender$gender, ref = "mixed")
relevelled_model <- lm(
  equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + mixed_reference,
  data = known_gender
)
coef(relevelled_model)
At the same season and requested amount, the all-men coefficient is about \(-0.121\) percentage points and the all-women coefficient about \(1.163\) percentage points. Both compare with mixed teams.
all.equal(fitted(gender_model), fitted(relevelled_model)) returns TRUE.
\(H_0:\beta_{all\_women}=\beta_{mixed}=0\) against the alternative that at least one of the two is not zero, with all-men as the reference group.
The unknown records have no known classification. Missing information is not a kind of team.
It confuses percent with percentage points, and it does not name the comparison group or what is held fixed. A precise version: “At the same season and requested amount, all-women presenting teams are fitted to offer 1.28 equity percentage points more than all-men presenting teams.”






Finish a half-worked example: a partial F with new numbers (10 minutes)
Test the two category dummies again, now in a smaller complete model. The reduced model contains only season:

reduced_season <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season, data = known_gender)
full_season    <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + gender,
                     data = known_gender)
anova(reduced_season, full_season)

Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: equity_offered_pct ~ season
Model 2: equity_offered_pct ~ season + gender
  Res.Df   RSS Df Sum of Sq      F   Pr(>F)   
1   1432 84646                                
2   1430 84003  2    643.43 5.4766 0.004272 **
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Step 1 (given). Adding the two dummies reduces the residual sum of squares by \(643.43\) using \(2\) degrees of freedom. The complete model leaves \(84{,}003\) on \(1{,}430\) degrees of freedom.
Step 2 (you). Plug these into the F formula from the worked example.
Step 3 (you). Compare with the table’s F and p-value and state the conclusion at 5% in one sentence.






Check your answer





\(F=(643.43/2)/(84{,}003/1{,}430)=321.7/58.7\approx 5.48\), matching the table, with p \(\approx\) 0.004. At 5%, the two category terms are jointly useful even in the model that adjusts only for season.





The 120-word interpretation (10 minutes)
Write an interpretation of the full gender_model in about 120 words. Include what the team categories do and do not record, and say why the result is not causal.






Check a model answer





A complete answer reports five things. First, the outcome and the sample: the equity offered, among the 1,434 broadcast pitches with a known team classification. Second, both estimates with units and with what is held fixed: all-women teams are fitted 1.28 percentage points above all-men teams and mixed teams 0.12 points above, at the same season and requested amount. Third, the uncertainty: p \(\approx\) 0.008 and 0.823 for the two coefficients, and p \(\approx\) 0.023 for the partial F-test, so the terms are jointly useful. Fourth, the limits of the measurement: the categories describe the people who presented, not shares of women or the full team. Fifth, the scope: these are adjusted associations among the recorded pitches, not causal effects.





Review: one question from Lecture 4 (5 minutes)
Using the Lecture 4 three-predictor model, compute the combined fitted difference for a pitch three seasons later requesting $200,000 more, at the same description length.






Check your answer





\(3(-0.836)+200(-0.0029)\approx-3.09\) percentage points. The two contributions add because the model is additive, and $200,000 is 200 units of ask_1k.





Worked exam interpretation (5 minutes)
Question. This question is in the style of Question 4 of the mock exam. A model of equity offered on season, ask_1k, and industry (four categories, reference Food and Beverage) reports industryTechnology 1.9 (p = 0.04). The numbers are invented. A student writes: “Technology pitches offer 1.9% more equity, so entering tech makes founders more generous.” Correct the sentence.






Check a model answer





Three corrections. Units: the estimate is 1.9 equity percentage points, not a relative 1.9%. Comparison and what is held fixed: technology pitches are fitted 1.9 points above Food and Beverage pitches at the same season and requested amount, among the recorded pitches. Scope: nothing here is causal. “Entering tech makes founders more generous” reads a comparison with the reference group as an effect of choosing an industry.





Check the AI (5 minutes)
You asked an AI assistant: “The coefficient of the all-women dummy is 1.28. What does that mean?” It answered:

“All-women teams offer 1.28% more equity than the average team.”

Find what is wrong and write the corrected answer. This is the Verify step of Attempt → Ask → Verify → Explain, and the exam asks for it.






Check your answer





Three errors. The unit is percentage points, not percent. The comparison is with the reference group, all-men teams, not with the average team. And it holds at the same season and requested amount. Correct: at the same season and requested amount, all-women teams are fitted to offer 1.28 percentage points more equity than all-men teams.





Make it yours (5 minutes)

Utility: two sentences
Think of your EiA3 venture, or any business you know well. Name one categorical feature of your customers or products (segment, channel, region, plan tier). Then write two sentences. Which category would you set as the reference group, and why? What would a “jointly useful” result of the F-test for the whole set of categories change in how you describe your market? There is no wrong answer.






See an example, then write your own





Take a student-run venture that sells meal-prep boxes on campus (an invented example). “My channels are the campus stand, the app, and the website. I would set the campus stand as the reference, because it is the first channel and every decision is compared with it. A jointly useful result of the F-test would justify describing my market by channel at all. Mixed p-values of the single dummies would not settle that.”



You can discuss this task, and any other task in this chapter, with Tilly, the course AI assistant. Ask it to check whether your two sentences confuse percent with percentage points, or to ask you questions about the dummy-variable trap with your own categories.

Continue to Lecture 6: Interactions and curvature.
Code sheet: Lecture 5 commands and formulas.
For a more formal treatment, see James et al., An Introduction to Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., Sections 3.2.2 and 3.3.1, and Nieuwenhuis, Statistical Methods for Business and Economics, Chapters 20–21.

title: Lecture 6: Interactions and curvature
text:
Before class
Total preparation time: about 30 minutes.
Minimum path: the video and the R task. Full path: everything in this section.
Bring a charged laptop with RStudio and the course project open. The code of the lecture is in this chapter, ready to copy, so you can run each step yourself during the lecture and get the same numbers and figures.
Derive the two lines (5 minutes). In the model \(Y=\beta_0+\beta_1X+\beta_2D+\beta_3XD+\varepsilon\) with a dummy variable \(D\in\{0,1\}\), write the line for \(D=0\) and the line for \(D=1\).
Predict (2 minutes). Answer the one-click Wooclap question posted on Canvas before you come to class: how many separate numbers do you need to fully describe a picture of two straight lines with different slopes? Choose one answer. You find the answer in the lecture material.
R warm-up (8 minutes). Build the variables for the analysis. The code uses the same known_gender subset as Lecture 5. It adds a dummy women and a centred season season_c, which is the season minus the mean season. It then fits one line of equity offered on season for each group and draws both lines. Bring the plot:
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
sharks$ask_1k <- sharks$ask_amount_usd / 1000
known_gender <- subset(sharks, pitcher_gender_group != "unknown")
known_gender$women <- as.integer(
  known_gender$pitcher_gender_group %in% c("all_women", "mixed")
)
known_gender$season_c <- known_gender$season - mean(known_gender$season)

plot(equity_offered_pct ~ season, data = known_gender,
     pch = 16, col = "grey80")
abline(lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season,
          data = subset(known_gender, women == 0)),
       col = "#0072B2", lwd = 3)
abline(lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season,
          data = subset(known_gender, women == 1)),
       col = "#D55E00", lwd = 3)
If you are not sure about products, powers, or centering, review Mathematics Refresher: products, powers, and centering.

title: Lecture 6: Interactions and curvature
text:
Video preparation (15 minutes) Watch Stanford Statistical Learning 3.5 Extensions of the Linear Model and 7.1 Polynomials and Step Functions. Focus on why an interaction changes a slope, and why a model with a squared term is still a linear regression. All links are also listed in the External Video Guide.








Check your preparation





For \(D=0\): \(E[Y\mid X,D=0]=\beta_0+\beta_1X\). For \(D=1\): \(E[Y\mid X,D=1]=(\beta_0+\beta_2)+(\beta_1+\beta_3)X\). Setting \(D=1\) shifts the intercept by \(\beta_2\) and the slope by \(\beta_3\).

title: Lecture 6: Interactions and curvature
text:
Lecture material
This section has two parts. The first part adds an interaction, which lets a slope differ between two groups. The second part adds a squared term, which lets a slope change along the predictor itself.

Stanford explanations (review): 3.5 Extensions of the Linear Model and 7.1 Polynomials and Step Functions.


Start with a founder’s question
Does advertising work equally well in every week? Does a trend go on in a straight line forever? Often the answer is “it depends”. The two tools of this lecture let you check this in the data. An interaction lets a slope differ between groups. A curve lets a slope change along the way.


The picture before the formula
In every model so far, all groups had the same slope. Lecture 5 let the height of the line differ between groups. Now the slope may differ as well. Start with the picture in Figure 23.1:


See the drawing code (optional, not exam material)
old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 1, 1), las = 1)
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 10), bty = "n",
     xlab = "Predictor X", ylab = "Outcome Y")
abline(a = 2, b = 0.75, col = "#009E73", lwd = 3)
abline(a = 4.5, b = 0.25, col = "#D55E00", lwd = 3, lty = 2)
text(8.4, 2 + 0.75 * 8.4 + 0.9, "Group D = 0", col = "#009E73")
text(8.4, 4.5 + 0.25 * 8.4 - 0.8, "Group D = 1", col = "#D55E00")
par(old_par)








Figure 23.1: Two groups, two lines, different slopes (an invented picture). How many numbers do you need to describe this picture completely?





This answers the Wooclap question from before class: four numbers, an intercept and a slope for each line. The interaction model writes the same four numbers in a different way:
\[
E[Y\mid X,D]
=\beta_0+\beta_1X+\beta_2D+\beta_3XD.
\]
Each coefficient is one feature of the picture:

\(\beta_0\): where the \(D=0\) line meets the vertical axis
\(\beta_1\): the slope of the \(D=0\) line
\(\beta_2\): how much higher the \(D=1\) line starts
\(\beta_3\): how much steeper the \(D=1\) line is.

The same in a table with one row per group, as you derived it before class:



Group
Intercept
Slope




\(D=0\)
\(\beta_0\)
\(\beta_1\)


\(D=1\)
\(\beta_0+\beta_2\)
\(\beta_1+\beta_3\)



When \(\beta_3=0\) the two lines are parallel, and the model is the dummy model of Lecture 5 with one common slope.


The interaction coefficient is a difference in slopes

Definition
Interaction. A term that is the product of two predictors, for example \(X\times D\). It lets the slope of one predictor depend on the value of the other. Its coefficient is a difference in slopes.

In the additive model the slope of \(X\) is the same at every value of the other predictor. With the product \(XD\) in the model, a one-unit increase in \(X\) changes the conditional mean by
\[
\beta_1+\beta_3D.
\]
So \(\beta_3\) is the difference between the slope of the group with \(D=1\) and the slope of the reference group. It is not an effect on its own. Its unit combines the two variables. If \(X\) is measured in seasons and \(D\) is a dummy, \(\beta_3\) is in outcome units per season: here, equity percentage points per season, one group minus the reference group. The same algebra works when the second variable is a number \(Z\) and not a dummy. The slope of \(X\) is then \(\beta_1+\beta_3Z\), a slope that changes with \(Z\).
Centering. Centering a predictor means subtracting its mean. With \(XD\) in the model, \(\beta_2\) compares the two groups at \(X=0\). For the Shark Tank data this would be Season 0, which does not exist. Replacing season with
\[
season\_c = season - \overline{season}
\]
moves that comparison to the average season (about 8.8). Centering changes one kind of thing and cannot change another:

It changes the meaning and the value of the intercept and of the group coefficient. Both now refer to the average season.
It cannot change the fitted values, the residuals, \(R^2\), or the interaction coefficient. The lines are the same lines. Only the place where we read the vertical gap between them has moved.







Check: which printed numbers change when season is centred?





The intercept and the women coefficient change. The interaction coefficient, the ask_1k coefficient, all fitted values, and \(R^2\) do not. You check this in R in the after-class practice.









Try it: two lines from four coefficients





Try this with your neighbour first. In an invented example, a venture models weekly orders with advertising spending in euros, a dummy for exam weeks, and their interaction: fitted orders = 100 + 0.10 × ads + 15 × exam + 0.12 × ads × exam.
Step 1 (given). In ordinary weeks (exam = 0) the line is 100 + 0.10 × ads.
Step 2 (you). Write the line for exam weeks.
Step 3 (you). Compare the fitted orders at 200 euros of advertising in the two kinds of weeks, and say what the coefficient 0.12 means.






Check your answer





Exam weeks: (100 + 15) + (0.10 + 0.12) × ads = 115 + 0.22 × ads. At 200 euros: 120 orders in an ordinary week and 159 in an exam week. The coefficient 0.12 is the difference between the two slopes: each euro of advertising goes with 0.12 more orders in an exam week than in an ordinary week.








The Shark Tank interaction model
Now take the first half of the driving question. In this lecture, women = 1 means that the presenting team is classified as all-women or mixed, and women = 0 means all-men. This split is broader than the three categories of Lecture 5. It does not measure the share of women or the full team behind the venture. The seven unknown records are left out as before. The code first builds the variables, as in the R warm-up:

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
sharks$ask_1k <- sharks$ask_amount_usd / 1000
known_gender <- subset(sharks, pitcher_gender_group != "unknown")
known_gender$women <- as.integer(
  known_gender$pitcher_gender_group %in% c("all_women", "mixed")
)
known_gender$season_c <- known_gender$season - mean(known_gender$season)

interaction_model <- lm(
  equity_offered_pct ~ season_c * women + ask_1k,
  data = known_gender
)
summary(interaction_model)


Call:
lm(formula = equity_offered_pct ~ season_c * women + ask_1k, 
    data = known_gender)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-15.871  -4.742  -1.290   3.412  82.689 

Coefficients:
                 Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)    13.6247907  0.3354522  40.616  < 2e-16 ***
season_c       -0.7993817  0.0663226 -12.053  < 2e-16 ***
women           0.8069665  0.4117061   1.960   0.0502 .  
ask_1k         -0.0026776  0.0005834  -4.590 4.83e-06 ***
season_c:women -0.0614594  0.0955667  -0.643   0.5203    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 7.62 on 1429 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.1894,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.1871 
F-statistic: 83.47 on 4 and 1429 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Use the table with one row per group to get the two season slopes, holding requested amount fixed. For all-men teams (women = 0), the fitted season slope is about \(-0.799\) percentage points per season. For teams with women (women = 1), it is
\[
-0.7994+(-0.0615)=-0.861
\text{ percentage points per season.}
\]
The interaction estimate is \(-0.061\) equity percentage points per season, with a p-value of about 0.520. The difference is small: about 8% of the all-men slope. Read this result in both directions. The model gives no evidence that the season trend differs between the two groups. It also does not prove that the two slopes are equal. The estimate is imprecise (standard error about 0.096), so the data fit a somewhat steeper trend and also a somewhat flatter trend for teams with women. No evidence of a difference is not proof of no difference.


See the R code for this figure
library(ggplot2)
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
sharks$ask_1k <- sharks$ask_amount_usd / 1000
known_gender <- subset(sharks, pitcher_gender_group != "unknown")
known_gender$women <- as.integer(
  known_gender$pitcher_gender_group %in% c("all_women", "mixed")
)
known_gender$season_c <- known_gender$season - mean(known_gender$season)
interaction_model <- lm(
  equity_offered_pct ~ season_c * women + ask_1k,
  data = known_gender
)
season_grid <- 1:16
ask_bar <- mean(known_gender$ask_1k)
newdat <- expand.grid(season = season_grid, women = c(0, 1))
newdat$season_c <- newdat$season - mean(known_gender$season)
newdat$ask_1k <- ask_bar
newdat$fit <- predict(interaction_model, newdata = newdat)
newdat$group <- ifelse(newdat$women == 1, "Women represented", "All-men")
fit_men_13 <- newdat$fit[newdat$women == 0 & newdat$season == 13]
fit_women_13 <- newdat$fit[newdat$women == 1 & newdat$season == 13]

ggplot(newdat, aes(x = season, y = fit,
                   colour = group, linetype = group)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(data = subset(newdat, season %in% c(1, 16)), size = 2.2) +
  annotate("text", x = 13, y = fit_women_13 + 1.1,
           label = "Women represented",
           colour = "#D55E00", size = 3.4) +
  annotate("text", x = 13, y = fit_men_13 - 1.1,
           label = "All-men",
           colour = "#009E73", size = 3.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("All-men" = "#009E73",
                                 "Women represented" = "#D55E00"),
                      guide = "none") +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("All-men" = "solid",
                                   "Women represented" = "dashed"),
                        guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, 16, by = 3)) +
  labs(x = "Season", y = "Fitted initial equity offered (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D")
  )








Figure 23.2: Fitted equity offered by season for all-men teams and for teams with women, at the average requested amount. The two lines are almost parallel. The slope of a line is the fitted change per season for that group, and the vertical gap is the fitted difference between the groups in a given season.





Always graph a model that contains an interaction. In Figure 23.2 the two almost parallel lines are the result. Once \(XD\) is in the model, neither \(\hat\beta_1\) nor \(\hat\beta_2\) alone describes all teams.


The hierarchy principle and the * shorthand
The hierarchy principle says: if a model contains \(XD\), keep both \(X\) and \(D\) in the model, even when one of them is not significant on its own. The terms \(X\) and \(D\) define the two lines, and the interaction describes the difference between these lines. Without one of them the two lines are restricted for no reason, for example to the same intercept, and this restriction distorts the interaction coefficient. The * shorthand in an R formula follows the principle for you:

lm(y ~ x * z, data = df)  # x * z expands to x + z + x:z

The first part of this lecture let the slope differ by group. The second part lets the slope differ along \(x\) itself. Both parts do the same thing: they give least squares a new column that is built from the data (a product or a square), and they read several coefficients together.


Curvature: polynomials are still linear regression
Is the season trend a straight line at all? To let it bend, add the square of the predictor.

Definition
Quadratic term. The square of a predictor, \(x^2\), added to a model that also contains \(x\). It lets the fitted line bend, so the slope changes with \(x\). A model with powers of a predictor is called a polynomial.

The quadratic conditional mean
\[
E[Y\mid X=x]=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2
\]
is curved in \(x\), but it is linear in the unknown coefficients \(\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2\). That is all lm() requires. The square is one more column of data.
What changes is how to read the output. The slope is no longer one number. Moving from \(x\) to \(x+1\) changes the conditional mean by
\[
(\beta_1(x+1)+\beta_2(x+1)^2) - (\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2)
=\beta_1+\beta_2(2x+1).
\]
This change depends on where you start. The rule is: never read \(\beta_1\) alone while \(x^2\) is in the model. Calculate fitted changes or graph the curve.

linear_season <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k, data = sharks)
poly_season <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k,
                  data = sharks)
summary(poly_season)$coefficients

                Estimate   Std. Error   t value      Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 24.171680818 0.8205664983 29.457309 1.332051e-149
season      -1.713233277 0.2056686354 -8.330066  1.862369e-16
I(season^2)  0.051034200 0.0113694269  4.488722  7.737227e-06
ask_1k      -0.002710806 0.0005740121 -4.722559  2.556506e-06


I() tells R to calculate the square. Without it, R would read ^ as formula syntax. The fitted coefficients are \(\hat\beta_1 \approx -1.713\) for season and \(\hat\beta_2 \approx 0.051\) for I(season^2). Together they describe a steep decline in the early seasons that becomes flatter season by season.

Example 23.1 (Worked example: the fitted change from Season 5 to Season 6) Holding requested amount fixed, the fitted change from season \(x\) to season \(x+1\) is \(\hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_2(2x+1)\). From Season 5 to Season 6, \(x = 5\):
\[
\hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_2(2\times5+1)
=-1.713+0.051\times11
=-1.713+0.561
\approx-1.15
\text{ percentage points.}
\]
Reading \(\hat\beta_1=-1.713\) alone would overstate the drop by about 0.56 points, which is about half of the fitted drop of 1.15 points. The number \(-1.713\) is not a constant slope. It belongs to \(x=0\), a season that does not exist. Check the calculation in R with the stored coefficients:

b <- coef(poly_season)
unname(b["season"] + b["I(season^2)"] * (2 * 5 + 1))

[1] -1.151857





Is the curvature worth having? The partial F
The quadratic model and the linear model are nested, so the partial F-test of Lecture 5 applies to the one added term:

anova(linear_season, poly_season)

Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k
Model 2: equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k
  Res.Df   RSS Df Sum of Sq      F    Pr(>F)    
1   1438 83493                                  
2   1437 82338  1    1154.5 20.149 7.737e-06 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The partial F-test for adding I(season^2) gives \(F \approx 20.1\) with a p-value below 0.001. The data show a curve. The gain in fit is small: adjusted \(R^2\) rises from about 0.186 to about 0.196, one percentage point more of the variation in the equity offered. So also look at the shape of the curve in Figure 23.3:


See the R code for this figure
library(ggplot2)
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
sharks$ask_1k <- sharks$ask_amount_usd / 1000
poly_season <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k,
                  data = sharks)
season_means <- aggregate(equity_offered_pct ~ season, data = sharks, mean)
curve_data <- data.frame(season = seq(1, 16, length.out = 200),
                         ask_1k = mean(sharks$ask_1k))
curve_data$fit <- predict(poly_season, newdata = curve_data)

ggplot(season_means, aes(x = season, y = equity_offered_pct)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 16, xmax = 17.6, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "grey75", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 16, colour = "grey60",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = curve_data, aes(x = season, y = fit),
            colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 2.6, colour = "#009E73") +
  annotate("text", x = 16.8, y = max(season_means$equity_offered_pct),
           label = "no data beyond\nseason 16", colour = "#5B6976",
           size = 3, lineheight = 0.95) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1, 16, by = 3)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(1, 17.6)) +
  labs(x = "Season", y = "Initial equity offered (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D")
  )








Figure 23.3: Season means of the equity offered (points) and the fitted quadratic curve at the average requested amount. The curve becomes flatter towards the last observed seasons. Beyond Season 16 (shaded) it would turn upward, but there are no data in that region.





The points in Figure 23.3 are the plain means of each season. The curve holds the requested amount at its sample mean. To extrapolate means to use a fitted model outside the range of the data. Do not extrapolate the quadratic beyond Seasons 1–16. The fitted curve reaches its lowest point just after Season 16 and would rise steeply afterwards. This rise comes from the shape of a quadratic, not from any data, so it is not a forecast.

What flexible terms can and cannot repair

Interactions and curves make the model more flexible. They repair nothing about how the data came about.
Every added term costs precision. Add a term because a question asks for it, not because it turns out significant.
A curve can be trusted only inside the range of the data.

What you can do with it: ask whether a relationship could differ between groups or bend, add that one term, graph the fitted lines, and report combined results.



Answering the driving question
The same trend for every kind of team? The estimated difference in slopes is \(-0.061\) percentage points per season (p \(\approx\) 0.52). The data show no difference between all-men teams and teams with women. They also do not prove that the trends are equal, because the estimate is imprecise.
A straight line? Not quite. The quadratic term is significant (partial \(F \approx 20.1\), p \(<\) 0.001). The fitted decline becomes flatter: from about \(-1.56\) points per season between Seasons 1 and 2 to about \(-0.64\) between Seasons 10 and 11. The curve can be used only inside Seasons 1–16.

A founder’s decision (invented example)
You suspect that advertising works better in exam weeks. The model with an interaction gives an advertising slope of 0.10 orders per euro in ordinary weeks and 0.10 + 0.12 = 0.22 in exam weeks. After a price increase, each order now brings 6 euros of margin. So 100 euros of advertising goes with 10 more orders and 60 euros of margin in an ordinary week, which is less than the advertising costs. In an exam week it goes with 22 more orders and 132 euros of margin. The decision: advertise in the exam weeks only. One check first: the interaction of 0.12 has its own interval. If that interval includes zero, the difference between the two kinds of weeks is not yet established, and you keep the budget split for one more term before you commit.

Next: Tutorial 2 practises Lectures 4–6 in the format of the exam. It ends with one full analysis, from a research question to a conclusion of 150 words. The exam asks for this kind of analysis, and so will your thesis.

title: Lecture 6: Interactions and curvature
text:
After class
Total practice time: about 85 minutes.
Minimum path (about 35 minutes): read the lecture material, answer the recall questions, then work for 10 minutes on the tasks that follow. Full path: all tasks below.

Read the lecture material (15 minutes)
Read the Lecture material section above from start to end. The lecture covered the core of it. The text has every step, every example, and all the code, including parts that were not shown in class. Note what is still unclear and bring it to the next tutorial, or ask Tilly.


Recall questions (10 minutes)

What does an interaction coefficient measure, and what is its unit in the model with season and the women dummy?
Why centre a predictor before you use it in an interaction, and what can centering never change?
State the hierarchy principle.
Why is a quadratic model still a linear regression model?
Why should you graph a quadratic curve, and why should you not extrapolate it?







Check your answers






How the slope of one predictor differs with the other predictor. Here its unit is equity percentage points per season, as a difference between the two groups.
So that the intercept and the group coefficient refer to a useful value, such as the sample mean, and not to zero. Centering never changes the fitted values, the residuals, \(R^2\), or the interaction coefficient.
Keep \(X\) and \(D\) in the model whenever their interaction \(XD\) is in it, and keep \(x\) whenever \(x^2\) is in it.
It is linear in the unknown coefficients. The squared column is one more predictor built from the data.
No single coefficient is the slope, so only fitted values or the curve show what the model says. Outside the observed range the curve can turn sharply, and no data support that turn.






Centering verification (10 minutes)
Fit the interaction model with and without centering season. Check that the fitted values and the interaction coefficient are unchanged, and report which coefficients do change.






Check your answer






sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
sharks$ask_1k <- sharks$ask_amount_usd / 1000
known_gender <- subset(sharks, pitcher_gender_group != "unknown")
known_gender$women <- as.integer(
  known_gender$pitcher_gender_group %in% c("all_women", "mixed")
)
known_gender$season_c <- known_gender$season - mean(known_gender$season)

uncentered <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season * women + ask_1k,
                 data = known_gender)
centered <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season_c * women + ask_1k,
               data = known_gender)
all.equal(fitted(uncentered), fitted(centered))

[1] TRUE

c(uncentered = unname(coef(uncentered)["season:women"]),
  centered = unname(coef(centered)["season_c:women"]))

 uncentered    centered 
-0.06145941 -0.06145941 

c(women_uncentered = unname(coef(uncentered)["women"]),
  women_centered = unname(coef(centered)["women"]))

women_uncentered   women_centered 
       1.3465150        0.8069665 


The fitted values agree, and both interaction estimates are about \(-0.061\). The women coefficient changes from about \(1.35\) (a comparison at Season 0, which does not exist) to about \(0.81\) (a comparison at the average season, about 8.8). The intercept changes as well. Centering moved the place where the gap is read. It did not move the lines.





Finish a half-worked example: a quadratic change (15 minutes)
Read the worked calculation for Season 5 to Season 6 again (Example 23.1). Then calculate the fitted change from Season 10 to Season 11 in the same model.
Step 1 (given). The formula is \(\hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_2(2x+1)\) with \(x=10\), so \(\hat\beta_2\) is multiplied by \(21\).
Step 2 (you). Plug in \(\hat\beta_1\approx-1.713\) and \(\hat\beta_2\approx0.051\).
Step 3 (you). Compare the result with the Season 5 to 6 change and state in one sentence what the comparison shows about the trend.






Check your answer





\(-1.713+0.051\times21\approx-1.713+1.071\approx-0.64\) percentage points (with the unrounded coefficients: \(\hat\beta_1+21\hat\beta_2=-0.642\)). The drop per season has become smaller, from about \(-1.15\) (Seasons 5–6) to about \(-0.64\) (Seasons 10–11). The decline becomes flatter in later seasons. This is what a positive \(\hat\beta_2\) means.



Now do the next tasks on your own, with new coefficients from an invented example. A model of monthly revenue (€1,000s) on the age of a shop \(x\) (years) reports \(\widehat Y = 40 - 2.00x + 0.060x^2\).

Calculate the fitted change from age 3 to age 4 and from age 8 to age 9.
A colleague reports “revenue falls €2,000 per year of age.” Correct the sentence.
In \(\widehat Y=10+2X+3D-0.5XD\), write the lines of both groups and interpret the interaction coefficient.







Check your answers






Age 3 to 4: \(-2.00+0.060(2\times3+1)=-2.00+0.42=-1.58\), about \(-€1{,}580\). Age 8 to 9: \(-2.00+0.060\times17=-0.98\), about \(-€980\).
\(-2.00\) is not the fitted change per year. With \(x^2\) in the model the change depends on age: about \(-1.58\) from age 3 to 4 and about \(-0.98\) from age 8 to 9. The decline becomes weaker as shops get older.
For \(D=0\): \(\widehat Y=10+2X\). For \(D=1\): \(\widehat Y=13+1.5X\). The interaction coefficient \(-0.5\) says that the slope of the \(D=1\) group is 0.5 outcome units per unit of \(X\) smaller than the slope of the \(D=0\) group.






Cumulative mini-task (15 minutes)
In Lecture 4 you wrote a paragraph that connects the diagnostics of Lecture 2 to the three-predictor model of the equity offered. Add one argument to that paragraph. Propose either an interaction or a quadratic term for that model. State the question about the business or the data that motivates the term, and say how you would test whether the term belongs in the model.






Check a model answer





A good answer: “The decline over the seasons need not be a straight line. The show was new in the early seasons and pitches became more professional later, so the trend may become flatter. I would add I(season^2). I add the term because of this question about the shape, not because I am searching for a significant result. I would test it with a partial F-test against the nested linear model on the same observations (here \(F\approx20.1\), p \(<\) 0.001), check that adjusted \(R^2\) rises, graph the fitted curve inside Seasons 1–16, and report fitted changes from season to season in place of the season coefficient alone.” An answer with an interaction is equally good if it names the question and the nested test. An example is the interaction of season with the women dummy, which asks whether the trend differs between the groups. Its test gives \(F\approx0.41\) and p \(\approx\) 0.52, so the term is not kept.





Review: one partial-F question from Lecture 5 (5 minutes)
Adding the two gender dummies to the season-and-ask model of equity reduced the residual sum of squares by 436.25 using 2 degrees of freedom, and the complete model left 82,792 on 1,429 degrees of freedom. Compute the partial F statistic and state the 5% conclusion.






Check your answer





\(F=(436.25/2)/(82{,}792/1{,}429)=218.1/57.9\approx3.76\), with p \(\approx\) 0.023. At 5%, the two category terms are jointly useful in that model, even though the t-test of the mixed dummy alone is far from significant. Joint tests and individual tests answer different questions.





Worked exam interpretation (5 minutes)
Question. This question is in the style of Question 5 of the mock exam. The numbers are invented. A model of the sales growth of ventures (percentage points) on marketing spending (€10,000s), a dummy for online-only ventures, and their interaction reports spending 1.20, online 2.00, spending:online -0.50. A student writes: “Spending raises growth by 1.2 percentage points per €10,000 for all ventures.” Correct the sentence.






Check a model answer





Two corrections. First, with the interaction in the model, 1.20 is the fitted spending slope only for ventures that are not online-only (online = 0). For online-only ventures the slope is \(1.20-0.50=0.70\) percentage points per €10,000. There is no single slope for all ventures. Second, “raises” claims causation. These are fitted associations among the sampled ventures, holding the other included terms fixed. The data do not come from an experiment, so they do not show an effect of spending.





Check the AI (5 minutes)
You asked an AI assistant: “The interaction has a coefficient of -0.061 and a p-value of 0.52. What do I conclude?” It answered:

“The p-value proves that the season trend is identical for both groups. And the season coefficient of -0.80 is the season trend for all teams.”

Find what is wrong and write the corrected answer. This is the Verify step of Attempt → Ask → Verify → Explain, and the exam asks for it.






Check your answer





Two errors. A large p-value means the data do not show a difference. It does not prove that the trends are the same, because the estimate is imprecise. And with an interaction in the model, -0.80 is the trend for the group coded 0, the all-men teams. For teams with women it is -0.80 - 0.06 = -0.86.





Make it yours (5 minutes)

Utility: two sentences
Think of your EiA3 venture, or any business you know well. Name one relationship in its data whose slope could depend on something else. For example, the response to price may differ by customer segment, the result of a campaign may differ by channel, or growth may become flatter as the business gets larger. Then write two sentences. First, state the interaction or quadratic term you would add and the question behind it. Second, say what a result that is not significant would tell you, and what it would not tell you. There is no wrong answer.






See an example, then write your own





Take a student-run venture that sells meal-prep boxes on campus (an invented example). “I would add an interaction of advertising spend with exam week, because my question is whether ads only work when students are on campus. An interaction that is not significant would mean no evidence that the slopes differ. It would not prove that exam weeks make no difference.”



You can discuss this task, and any other task in this chapter, with Tilly, the course AI assistant. Ask it to read your two sentences and to check whether you treated “no evidence of a difference” as “proof of no difference”.

Continue to Tutorial 2: Multiple regression and extensions.
Code sheet: Lecture 6 commands and formulas.
For a more formal treatment, see James et al., An Introduction to Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., Section 3.3.2 and Sections 3.6.4–3.6.6, and Nieuwenhuis, Statistical Methods for Business and Economics, Chapter 21.

title: Tutorial 2: Multiple regression and extensions
text:
In the tutorial
Try each task in R before you open the answer. Tasks 1 to 4 use the Shark Tank file, and money is measured in thousands of dollars (ask_1k). First build the data for the analysis. The code is the same as in Lectures 4–6:

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
sharks$ask_1k <- sharks$ask_amount_usd / 1000
known_gender <- subset(sharks, pitcher_gender_group != "unknown")
known_gender$gender <- relevel(factor(known_gender$pitcher_gender_group),
                               ref = "all_men")
known_gender$ask_1k <- known_gender$ask_amount_usd / 1000
known_gender$women <- as.integer(
  known_gender$pitcher_gender_group %in% c("all_women", "mixed")
)
known_gender$season_c <- known_gender$season - mean(known_gender$season)


Task 1: Multiple-regression coefficients (Lecture 4)
Fit:

m1 <- lm(
  equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + description_words,
  data = sharks
)
summary(m1)

    data = sharks)

Residuals:

-15.295  -4.776  -1.283   3.288  82.106

Multiple R-squared:  0.1876,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.1859 
F-statistic: 110.6 on 3 and 1437 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16



Interpret all three slopes with units and with the predictors that are held fixed.
Find out which 95% confidence interval of a coefficient includes zero.
Interpret adjusted \(R^2\) and the overall F-test.
Give two reasons why the coefficients cannot be read as causal effects.







Check your answer





At fixed values of the other included predictors, among the 1,441 recorded pitches: one later season is associated with about 0.836 percentage points less equity offered, an extra $1,000 requested with about 0.0029 percentage points less (about 0.29 points per $100,000), and one additional description word with about 0.128 percentage points less. confint(m1) shows that the interval for the description words, about \((-0.351, 0.095)\), includes zero. Adjusted \(R^2\approx0.186\): the model accounts for about 19% of the variation in the equity offered. The overall F-test (\(F\approx110.6\) on 3 and 1437 df) rejects the null hypothesis that all three slopes are zero. Possible reasons against a causal reading: only selected pitches reach the show, the quality of the venture is not measured, the equity offered may influence the amount requested, and the variables may be measured with error.





Task 2: Dummy variables and a partial F-test (Lecture 5)

              data = known_gender)
complete <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + gender,

Name the reference category.
Interpret both dummy coefficients.
State the hypotheses of the partial F-test and decide.
Explain why the partial F-test and the individual t-tests answer different questions.







Check your answer





The reference category is all-men. At the same season and requested amount, all-women presenting teams are fitted to offer about 1.28 equity percentage points more than all-men teams, and mixed teams about 0.12 points more. The unit is percentage points, not percent. The null hypothesis of the partial F-test is that both dummy coefficients are zero. \(F\approx3.76\) and p \(\approx\) 0.023, so reject at 5%. The two terms are jointly useful, even though the t-test of the mixed dummy alone (p \(\approx\) 0.82) is far from significant. The F-test asks whether the two terms together improve the model. Each t-test asks about one comparison with the reference group. The categories are broad and the data do not come from an experiment, so the result does not show a causal effect of gender.





Task 3: Interaction (Lecture 6)

m_interaction <- lm(
  equity_offered_pct ~ season_c * women + ask_1k,
  data = known_gender
)
summary(m_interaction)

F-statistic: 83.47 on 4 and 1429 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16



Write the fitted line for women = 0 and for women = 1 at a fixed requested amount.
Calculate both season slopes.
Interpret the interaction estimate and its p-value without claiming too much in either direction.
Explain what centering does.







Check your answer





At a fixed requested amount, the fitted line for all-men teams is \(13.625-0.799\,season\_c\) plus the term for the requested amount. For teams with women the intercept is \(13.625+0.807=14.432\) and the slope is \(-0.7994-0.0615=-0.861\). So the season slope is about \(-0.799\) percentage points per season for all-men teams and about \(-0.861\) for teams with women. The estimated difference in slopes is \(-0.061\) percentage points per season with p \(\approx\) 0.520. The model gives no evidence that the season trends differ between the two groups. It also does not prove that the trends are equal, because the estimate is imprecise. Centering makes the women coefficient compare the groups at the average season (about 8.8) and not at Season 0, which does not exist. It changes neither the fitted values nor the interaction estimate.





Task 4: Polynomial term (Lecture 6)

m_linear <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k, data = sharks)
m_quadratic <- lm(

Why must I(season^2) be used in the R formula?
Decide with the partial F-test whether the quadratic term improves the model.
Calculate the fitted change from Season 10 to Season 11.
State why the curve should not be extrapolated beyond Season 16.







Check your answer





I() tells R to calculate the square. Without it, R would read ^ as formula syntax. The partial F-test gives \(F\approx20.1\) with p \(<\) 0.001, so the quadratic term improves the model. With \(\hat\beta_1\approx-1.713\) and \(\hat\beta_2\approx0.051\), the change from Season 10 to 11 is \(\hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_2(2\times10+1)=\hat\beta_1+21\hat\beta_2\approx-0.64\) percentage points. Never read \(\hat\beta_1\) alone while the squared term is in the model. Beyond Season 16 the fitted curve turns upward, and no data support that turn. A quadratic curve can change direction sharply outside the observed range.

Entrepreneurial self-efficacy (1–7)

0.38***




(0.07)


Observations
265

\(R^2\)

Adjusted \(R^2\)
0.02
