Outcome: entrepreneurial intention (scale from 1 to 7). Ordinary least squares. Standard errors in parentheses. * p < 0.05, ** p < 0.01, *** p < 0.001.

What do the numbers in parentheses and the stars mean? Check the stars of the self-efficacy coefficient with its t statistic.
Interpret the self-efficacy coefficient in column (2) in one complete sentence.
The coefficient of Female changes from \(-0.21\) with a star in column (1) to \(-0.15\) without a star in column (2). Explain what happened with the ideas of Lecture 4, and say what the missing star does and does not mean.
\(R^2\) rises from 0.03 to 0.19. What does that say, and which test would judge whether the two added predictors are jointly useful?







Check your answer






The numbers in parentheses are standard errors. The stars show the p-value of the two-sided t-test of each coefficient against zero. For self-efficacy, \(t=0.38/0.07\approx5.4\). This is far beyond the multiplier \(t_{0.975,\,260}\approx1.97\), and p is below 0.001, so three stars are correct.
Among the 265 surveyed students, a self-efficacy score that is one point higher is associated with an entrepreneurial intention that is 0.38 points higher, holding age, gender, and prior experience fixed.
Model (2) holds two more variables fixed than model (1). The Female coefficient now compares women and men with the same experience and self-efficacy. Part of the raw gap of 0.21 points went together with differences in those two variables. The missing star says that the confidence interval around \(-0.15\) includes zero. It does not show that the gap is zero.
The two added predictors account for a further 16 percentage points of the variation in intentions in this sample. A partial F-test of the two nested models, anova(reduced, complete), would judge whether they are jointly useful.
crumbs: 24  Tutorial 2: Multiple regression and extensions

title: Tutorial 2: Multiple regression and extensions
text:
After class

Timed integrated task: 30 minutes
Build one model of the equity offered (equity_offered_pct) in the Shark Tank file. Use season, the requested amount in $1,000s, the three known categories of presenting teams, and one extension that you can justify: an interaction or a quadratic term.
Your answer must include:

a precise research question
the code that prepares the data, so that someone else can repeat it
one graph of the data before you fit the model
the R formula and the model summary. If you compare several models, show them in one regression table in the layout of this tutorial
interpretations of the coefficients with units and reference groups
a t-test of one coefficient and an overall or partial F-test
\(R^2\), adjusted \(R^2\), and residual diagnostics
one graph of fitted values from the model
a conclusion of 150 words that keeps apart the association, its uncertainty, and the reasons why it is not causal.







Check a model structure





A good solution could fit
m <- lm(
  equity_offered_pct ~ season * gender + ask_1k,
  data = known_gender
)
or a model with a quadratic term for season and the group dummies. Keep season and gender in the model next to their interaction (the hierarchy principle), and name the reference group. Interpret slopes that combine several coefficients, or differences between fitted values. Compare the model with a nested reduced model with anova(reduced, complete). Inspect the residuals, including rstandard() and Cook’s distance, and plot fitted values inside Seasons 1–16. The conclusion must say that the team categories are broad, that only broadcast pitches are in the file, and that the results therefore do not show a causal effect of gender or season.





Make it yours (5 minutes)

Utility: two sentences
Think of your EiA3 venture, or any business you know well. Describe in two sentences the full analysis that you would run on its data. First, name the outcome, two predictors, and one extension (a set of dummies, an interaction, or a quadratic term) that a real question motivates. Second, say which limit you would put first in your conclusion: selection, measurement, or omitted variables. There is no wrong answer.






See an example, then write your own





Take a student-run venture that sells meal-prep boxes on campus (an invented example). “Outcome: weekly orders. Predictors: advertising spend and price, plus a dummy for exam weeks and its interaction with advertising spend, because I believe ads work mainly when students are on campus. The first limit is omitted variables: the weather drives both how many flyers I hand out and how many people are on campus, and nothing in my data measures it.”



You can discuss this task, and any other task in this tutorial, with Tilly, the course AI assistant. Ask it to review your two sentences before you spend a weekend on the data.

QM Intermediate is complete. Review the QM Intermediate Code Sheet, attempt the QM Intermediate Mock Exam, then return to the R Refresher, Mathematics Refresher, or the External Video Guide whenever you need a targeted review.

title: QM Intermediate Code Sheet
text:
This sheet collects the R commands and formulas of QM Intermediate, ordered by lecture. The names y, x, group, and df are placeholders. Replace them by the variables and the dataset of the exam question.
The code sheet is provided at the exam. The table shows which sections you need when.
The sheet helps with R syntax and with calculations. You must still define the sample, check the assumptions, interpret units and reference categories, and tell association from causation.
For a more formal explanation of regression, inference, extensions, and violations of the assumptions, consult Nieuwenhuis, Statistical Methods for Business and Economics, Chapters 19–22.
Continue to the QM Intermediate Mock Exam.

title: QM Intermediate Code Sheet
text:
Workflow and data checks
df <- read.csv("data.csv")

dim(df)
names(df)
head(df)
str(df)
summary(df)
colSums(is.na(df))
table(df$group, useNA = "ifany")
Create new variables in visible code. Put money in readable units (this course uses millions or thousands of dollars). When you compare models, fit them all on the same observations:
df$x_1k <- df$x_euros / 1000
df$group <- factor(df$group)
df$group <- relevel(df$group, ref = "reference")

needed <- c("y", "x1", "x2", "group")
analysis <- df[complete.cases(df[needed]), ]
For every exam analysis:

Say what one row is, and name the outcome, the predictors, their units, and the sample.
Inspect the values and check for missing values.
Make a graph that fits the variables.
Fit the model and check its diagnostics.
Report the estimates, their uncertainty, the fit, and the relevant test.
Interpret the results in context, and state the limits that come from the sample and the reasons why a result is or is not causal.

title: QM Intermediate Code Sheet
text:
Lecture 1: Simple linear regression
The population model and fitted line are
\[
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
\widehat Y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1X_i.
\]
For simple OLS,
\[
\hat\beta_1=
\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}
{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2}
=\frac{s_{XY}}{s_X^2}
=r_{XY}\,\frac{s_Y}{s_X},
\qquad
\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x.
\]
The residual and least-squares criterion are
\[
e_i=Y_i-\widehat Y_i,
\qquad
\operatorname{SSE}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}e_i^2.
\]
Fit and inspect a simple regression:
m <- lm(y ~ x, data = df)
coef(m)
summary(m)

fitted(m)
residuals(m)
Plot the observations and fitted line:
plot(y ~ x, data = df,
     xlab = "Predictor (unit)", ylab = "Outcome (unit)")
abline(m, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
Calculate a fitted value or ask R for fitted conditional means:
b <- coef(m)
b[1] + b[2] * x0

new_cases <- data.frame(x = c(x0, x1))
predict(m, newdata = new_cases)
predict(m, newdata = new_cases, interval = "confidence")
Interpret \(\hat\beta_1\) as the fitted change in the outcome for a one-unit increase in the predictor. State both units, and write “associated with” unless the data come from an experiment. Rescaling both variables by the same factor changes the intercept and leaves the slope unchanged. Multiplying only the outcome by a factor multiplies the slope by it. Multiplying only the predictor by a factor divides the slope by it (see the worked example on units in Lecture 1).

title: QM Intermediate Code Sheet
section: Lecture 2: Assumptions, residual diagnostics, and influence
text:
Lecture 2: Assumptions, residual diagnostics, and influence
The diagnostic plots check the assumptions in the table of Lecture 2. A curve in the residual plot puts the linear conditional mean in doubt. A fan shape puts the constant conditional variance in doubt. Large standardised residuals or large Cook’s distances flag observations that you must investigate. Plots cannot show independence, the absence of confounding, the quality of the measurement, or causality. These depend on how the data were collected.
Make the two main diagnostic plots:
plot(fitted(m), residuals(m),
     xlab = "Fitted value", ylab = "Residual")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)

qqnorm(rstandard(m))
qqline(rstandard(m))
Find unusual and influential observations. Lecture 2 explains the first five commands (nobs(m) is the number of observations \(n\)). The three plot(m, which = ...) lines are shortcuts that draw the residual plot, the Q–Q plot, and a plot of Cook’s distance:
summary(residuals(m))         # summary of the residuals, a first check
rstandard(m)                  # standardised residuals, beyond about ±3 is large
cooks.distance(m)             # influence, a common threshold is 4/n
sum(abs(rstandard(m)) > 3)
sum(cooks.distance(m) > 4 / nobs(m))

plot(m, which = 1)  # residuals versus fitted
plot(m, which = 2)  # normal Q--Q
plot(m, which = 4)  # Cook's distance
For a flagged observation: investigate it and report it. Never delete it without reporting.

title: QM Intermediate Code Sheet
section: Lecture 3: Coefficient inference, fit, and the F-test
text:
Lecture 3: Coefficient inference, fit, and the F-test
For a two-sided test against zero,
\[
H_0:\beta_j=0,
\qquad
H_1:\beta_j\ne0,
\qquad
t=\frac{\hat\beta_j}{\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\beta_j)}.
\]
With \(k\) slopes and an intercept, the residual degrees of freedom and the 95% confidence interval are
\[
df=n-k-1,
\qquad
\hat\beta_j\pm t_{0.975,\,df}\,\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\beta_j).
\]
In simple regression, \(k=1\) and \(df=n-2\). The multiplier \(t_{0.975,\,df}\) is qt(0.975, df) in R.
summary(m)                 # estimates, SEs, t tests, p-values, fit
confint(m, level = 0.95)   # coefficient confidence intervals
df.residual(m)
nobs(m)
qt(0.975, df.residual(m))  # multiplier for a 95% interval
To verify R’s two-sided test against zero:
tab <- summary(m)$coefficients
t_value <- tab["x", "Estimate"] / tab["x", "Std. Error"]
p_value <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_value), df = df.residual(m))
The decomposition of variation:
\[
\text{SST}=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2,\qquad
\text{SSE}=\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2,\qquad
\text{SSR}=\sum_i(\hat y_i-\bar y)^2,
\]
\[
\text{SST}=\text{SSR}+\text{SSE},
\qquad
R^2=1-\frac{\text{SSE}}{\text{SST}}
=\frac{\text{SSR}}{\text{SST}}.
\]
Calculate the components:
y <- model.response(model.frame(m))
yhat <- fitted(m)

SST <- sum((y - mean(y))^2)
SSE <- sum(residuals(m)^2)
SSR <- SST - SSE
R2 <- 1 - SSE / SST
Extract fit statistics:
summary(m)$r.squared
summary(m)$adj.r.squared
summary(m)$fstatistic
sigma(m)                    # residual standard error
The residual standard error and adjusted \(R^2\) are
\[
s=\sqrt{\frac{\text{SSE}}{n-k-1}},
\qquad
R^2_{\text{adjusted}}
=1-(1-R^2)\frac{n-1}{n-k-1}.
\]
For \(k\) slopes,
\[
F=\frac{\text{SSR}/k}{\text{SSE}/(n-k-1)}
\]
tests
\[
H_0:\beta_1=\cdots=\beta_k=0
\]
against the alternative that at least one slope is not zero. Read F as the explained variation per predictor, divided by the residual variation per residual degree of freedom. In simple regression, the overall \(F\) statistic equals the square of the t statistic of the slope. \(R^2\) is the share of the variation in this sample that the model explains. It is not evidence of causation, and it does not show how well the model predicts new data.
Robust standard errors and robust 95% confidence intervals (Lecture 3):
library(lmtest)
library(sandwich)

coeftest(m, vcov. = vcovHC(m, type = "HC1"))
coefci(m, vcov. = vcovHC(m, type = "HC1"))
Robust standard errors remain valid when the error variance is not constant. They do not repair a wrong shape of the model, they do not remove confounding, and they do not make a coefficient causal.

title: QM Intermediate Code Sheet
text:
Lecture 4: Multiple linear regression
\[
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_kX_{ik}+\varepsilon_i.
\]
m_multi <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, data = analysis)
summary(m_multi)
confint(m_multi)
Interpret \(\hat\beta_j\) as the fitted change in the outcome for a one-unit increase in \(X_j\), holding the other included predictors fixed. Include:

the estimate and its direction
the predictor step and its unit
the unit of the outcome
the predictors that are held fixed
the analysed sample, and “associated with” unless the data come from an experiment.

For changes \(\Delta x_1,\ldots,\Delta x_k\), the additive fitted difference is
\[
\Delta\widehat Y=\hat\beta_1\Delta x_1+\cdots+\hat\beta_k\Delta x_k.
\]
Use predict() to combine terms without manual arithmetic:
cases <- data.frame(
  x1 = c(x1_A, x1_B),
  x2 = c(x2_A, x2_B),
  x3 = c(x3_A, x3_B)
)
fits <- predict(m_multi, newdata = cases)
fits[2] - fits[1]
A regression table with one column per model, as in a research paper. You need this for your thesis, not at the exam. Install the package once with install.packages("modelsummary"). All models must use the same observations:
library(modelsummary)
m_a <- lm(y ~ x1, data = analysis)
m_b <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = analysis)
modelsummary(
  list("(1)" = m_a, "(2)" = m_b, "(3)" = m_multi),
  stars = c("*" = 0.05, "**" = 0.01, "***" = 0.001),
  gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared", "adj.r.squared")
)
modelsummary rounds to three decimals.

title: QM Intermediate Code Sheet
section: Lecture 5: Factors, reference categories, and partial F-tests
text:
Lecture 5: Factors, reference categories, and partial F-tests
Set a reference category before fitting:
analysis$group <- relevel(factor(analysis$group), ref = "reference")

m_group <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + group, data = analysis)
summary(m_group)
coef(m_group)
confint(m_group)
Each printed group coefficient compares that category with the reference category, holding the other included predictors fixed. Releveling changes which comparisons are reported. It does not change the fitted values:
analysis$group_alt <- relevel(analysis$group, ref = "other")
m_alt <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + group_alt, data = analysis)
all.equal(fitted(m_group), fitted(m_alt))
Compare nested models fitted to the same observations:
reduced <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = analysis)
complete <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + group, data = analysis)
anova(reduced, complete)
The partial F-test asks whether the coefficients of all terms that are left out of the reduced model are zero at the same time. The reduced model must be the complete model without some of its terms, and both models must use the same outcome and the same observations.
If the complete model has \(k_C\) slopes and the reduced model leaves out \(q\) of these terms,
\[
F=
\frac{(\text{SSE}_{R}-\text{SSE}_{C})/q}
{\text{SSE}_{C}/(n-k_C-1)}.
\]

title: QM Intermediate Code Sheet
text:
Lecture 6: Interactions and polynomial terms
For an interaction between a numerical predictor \(X\) and a dummy \(D\),
\[
\widehat Y=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1X+\hat\beta_2D+\hat\beta_3XD.
\]

\(D=0\): intercept \(\hat\beta_0\), slope \(\hat\beta_1\)
\(D=1\): intercept \(\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_2\), slope \(\hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_3\)
\(\hat\beta_3\): difference in slopes.

Use * to include \(X\), \(D\), and their interaction (the hierarchy principle):
m_interaction <- lm(y ~ x * group + z, data = analysis)
# x * group expands to x + group + x:group
summary(m_interaction)
Centering (subtracting the mean) changes the meaning of the intercept and of the group coefficient. It does not change the fitted values or the interaction estimate:
analysis$x_c <- analysis$x - mean(analysis$x)
m_centered <- lm(y ~ x_c * group + z, data = analysis)
For a quadratic model,
\[
\widehat Y=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1X+\hat\beta_2X^2,
\]
the change from \(x\) to \(x+1\) is \(\hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_2(2x+1)\), and more generally the fitted change from \(x_A\) to \(x_B\) is
\[
\Delta\widehat Y
=\hat\beta_1(x_B-x_A)+\hat\beta_2(x_B^2-x_A^2).
\]
m_linear <- lm(y ~ x + z, data = analysis)
m_quadratic <- lm(y ~ x + I(x^2) + z, data = analysis)

summary(m_quadratic)
anova(m_linear, m_quadratic)
I(x^2) tells R to calculate the square. Keep the term \(x\) in the model, never interpret \(\hat\beta_1\) alone while \(x^2\) is in the model, and do not use the curve beyond the observed range of \(x\).
Create fitted values for a graph:
grid <- expand.grid(
  x = seq(min(analysis$x), max(analysis$x), length.out = 100),
  group = levels(analysis$group),
  z = mean(analysis$z)
)

pred <- predict(m_interaction, newdata = grid, interval = "confidence")
plot_data <- cbind(grid, pred)

title: Mock Exam: QM Intermediate
text:
Dataset used throughout
This mock exam covers all six lectures of the course. It has 100 points, so the exam grade is
\[
\text{grade} = \frac{\text{points earned}}{10}.
\]
The Intermediate exam is taken in TestVision, with R available. The practice exam in TestVision appears in your own TestVision account once it is published. You log in with your university account. There is no separate link. General information about TestVision for students is on the university page about TestVision.
The QM Intermediate Code Sheet is provided at the exam. Use it to review the R commands and the formulas before you try this mock exam.
Unless a question says otherwise, use a 5% significance level. Interpret every coefficient in the units and for the sample defined below. Do not use causal language unless the way the data were produced supports it.
The exam dataset is simulated. Treat it as a simple random sample of 320 independent young ventures from a business registry. One row is one venture. The data are observational: none of the predictors was assigned by chance.
The population is the set of ventures in this registry. Later survival and market conditions are not measured.
The dataset is simulated with a fixed seed, so you can reproduce every printed result on this page exactly. The code below generates the data and fits the four models used in the questions:
set.seed(734)
n_mock <- 320
marketing_10k <- round(runif(n_mock, 0.25, 8), 2)
experience_years <- sample(0:18, n_mock, replace = TRUE)
team_size <- sample(
  1:10, n_mock, replace = TRUE,
  prob = c(8, 16, 20, 20, 14, 9, 6, 4, 2, 1)
)
digital <- factor(
  ifelse(runif(n_mock) < 0.45, "Yes", "No"),
  levels = c("No", "Yes")
)
spend_c <- marketing_10k - 4
growth_mean <-
  8 + 1.10 * spend_c + 3 * (digital == "Yes") -
  0.10 * spend_c^2 + 0.30 * experience_years +
  0.70 * spend_c * (digital == "Yes") + 0.20 * team_size
growth_pct <- round(
  growth_mean + rnorm(n_mock, 0, 2.5 + 0.40 * marketing_10k),
  2
)
ventures <- data.frame(
  growth_pct, marketing_10k, experience_years, team_size, digital, spend_c
)

simple_model <- lm(growth_pct ~ marketing_10k, data = ventures)
multiple_model <- lm(
  growth_pct ~ marketing_10k + experience_years + team_size + digital,
  data = ventures
)
additive_model <- lm(
  growth_pct ~ spend_c + digital + experience_years,
  data = ventures
)
extended_model <- lm(
  growth_pct ~ spend_c * digital + I(spend_c^2) + experience_years,
  data = ventures
)
Download qm-intermediate-mock-exam.csv, save it in your R project, and load it with:
The printed results below let you continue if R is not available for a moment. When you practise with a time limit, reproduce them from the downloaded file.

title: Mock Exam: QM Intermediate
section: Question 1: Simple regression and least squares (20 points)
text:
Question 1: Simple regression and least squares (20 points)
The first model is
simple_model <- lm(growth_pct ~ marketing_10k, data = ventures)
and R reports
Coefficients:
                Estimate  Std. Error  t value  Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)        6.60       0.52      12.72   <2e-16
marketing_10k      1.38       0.11      12.35   <2e-16

Residual standard error: 4.57 on 318 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared: 0.324

Write the fitted regression equation with units. (3 points)
Interpret the slope and intercept in context. Comment on whether the intercept has a useful meaning here. (6 points)
Calculate the fitted growth for a venture spending €30,000 on marketing. If its observed growth is 15 percentage points, calculate its residual and interpret the sign. (5 points)
Explain what least squares minimises and why residuals are squared rather than simply summed. (4 points)
State the observational unit and why the fitted slope is not automatically causal. (2 points)







Model answer and marking guide






\(\widehat{growth\_pct}=6.60+1.38\,marketing\_10k\), where the outcome is in percentage points and the predictor in €10,000s (3 points).
For each additional €10,000 of marketing spending, fitted annual sales growth is 1.38 percentage points higher among sampled ventures (3 points). At zero marketing spending, fitted growth is 6.60 percentage points (2 points). This intercept is useful only if zero lies in or near the observed spending range and defines a meaningful venture (1 point).
€30,000 gives marketing_10k = 3, so the fitted value is \(6.60+1.38(3)=10.74\) percentage points (3 points). The residual is \(15-10.74=4.26\) percentage points. Positive means observed growth exceeds the model’s fitted value (2 points).
Least squares chooses the coefficients that minimise the sum of squared residuals, \(\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2\) (2 points). Residuals that are not squared cancel: with an intercept, the positive and negative residuals sum to zero. Squaring also counts large misses more heavily (2 points).
The unit is one venture (1 point). An association in observational data can come from confounding, reverse causality, selection, or measurement error (1 point).

title: Mock Exam: QM Intermediate
text:
Question 2: Assumptions and diagnostics (20 points)
R produced the following diagnostics for lm(growth_pct ~ marketing_10k, data = ventures). In the left panel, each point has fitted growth on the horizontal axis and its residual on the vertical axis. In the right panel, observed standardised residuals are plotted against theoretical standard-normal quantiles. A normal pattern would follow the straight reference line.


See the R code for this figure
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
# Rebuilds the same ventures dataset as the visible chunk above (same seed).
set.seed(734)
n_mock <- 320
marketing_10k <- round(runif(n_mock, 0.25, 8), 2)
experience_years <- sample(0:18, n_mock, replace = TRUE)
team_size <- sample(
  1:10, n_mock, replace = TRUE,
  prob = c(8, 16, 20, 20, 14, 9, 6, 4, 2, 1)
)
digital <- factor(
  ifelse(runif(n_mock) < 0.45, "Yes", "No"),
  levels = c("No", "Yes")
)
spend_c <- marketing_10k - 4
growth_mean <-
  8 + 1.10 * spend_c + 3 * (digital == "Yes") -
  0.10 * spend_c^2 + 0.30 * experience_years +
  0.70 * spend_c * (digital == "Yes") + 0.20 * team_size
growth_pct <- round(
  growth_mean + rnorm(n_mock, 0, 2.5 + 0.40 * marketing_10k),
  2
)
ventures <- data.frame(
  growth_pct, marketing_10k, experience_years, team_size, digital, spend_c
)
simple_model <- lm(growth_pct ~ marketing_10k, data = ventures)

resid_df <- data.frame(
  fitted = fitted(simple_model),
  residual = residuals(simple_model)
)
qq_df <- data.frame(rs = rstandard(simple_model))
theme_mock <- theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"),
    axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D")
  )

p_resid <- ggplot(resid_df, aes(x = fitted, y = residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#C98B2E",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, size = 1.6, colour = "#009E73") +
  annotate("text", x = max(resid_df$fitted), y = 0,
           label = "residual = 0", hjust = 1, vjust = -0.7,
           colour = "#17324D", size = 3) +
  labs(x = "Fitted growth (percentage points)",
       y = "Residual (percentage points)") +
  theme_mock

p_qq <- ggplot(qq_df, aes(sample = rs)) +
  geom_qq_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_qq(colour = "#009E73", alpha = 0.45, size = 1.6) +
  labs(x = "Normal theoretical quantile",
       y = "Observed standardised residual") +
  theme_mock

p_resid + p_qq








Figure 26.1: Residual-versus-fitted plot and normal Q-Q plot for the simple model.






Read both axes of the residual-versus-fitted panel and explain what a point above zero represents. (4 points)
What pattern do you see in that panel? Name the assumption it challenges. (4 points)
Explain how to read the Q–Q plot and assess normality here. (4 points)
Name two regression assumptions that these plots cannot establish, and state what information would help assess each. (4 points)
Would heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors repair a curved conditional mean or make the slope causal? Explain. (4 points)







Model answer and marking guide






The horizontal axis is model-fitted growth. The vertical axis is observed-minus-fitted growth, both in percentage points (2 points). A point above zero is a venture whose observed growth is higher than its fitted growth (2 points).
Vertical spread increases with fitted growth, creating a fan shape (2 points). This challenges constant conditional variance (homoskedasticity) (2 points).
The Q–Q plot compares ordered residuals with values expected under a normal distribution. Agreement appears as points near the line (2 points). The middle is reasonably aligned but tail departures suggest imperfect normality and possible extreme residuals (2 points).
Examples. Independence: you need to know whether ventures are clustered, observed more than once, or sampled in a particular order. No confounding: you need knowledge of how the data came about and of relevant variables that are not in the model. Correct measurement: you need information about how the variables were recorded. (2 points for each valid assumption with the information that would help, maximum 4.)
Robust standard errors give better estimates of the uncertainty in large samples when the error variance is not constant (2 points). They do not change the fitted conditional mean, they do not repair a curve that the model leaves out, they do not remove confounding, and they do not make a coefficient from observational data causal (2 points).

title: Mock Exam: QM Intermediate
section: Question 3: Model fit and the overall F-test (20 points)
text:
Question 3: Model fit and the overall F-test (20 points)
The researcher next fits
multiple_model <- lm(
  growth_pct ~ marketing_10k + experience_years + team_size + digital,
  data = ventures
)
R reports:
Residual standard error: 4.09 on 315 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared: 0.464, Adjusted R-squared: 0.457
F-statistic: 68.10 on 4 and 315 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16
For the intercept-only model, SST = 9,831.91. For multiple_model, SSE = 5,272.57.

Verify \(R^2\) from SST and SSE. Interpret it precisely. (6 points)
Explain why adjusted \(R^2\) is lower than \(R^2\), and when adjusted \(R^2\) is useful. (4 points)
State the null and alternative hypotheses of the reported overall F-test. Give its conclusion. (6 points)
Explain why this F-test is not equivalent to four separate 5% t-tests. (2 points)
Does \(R^2=0.464\) show that the model predicts future ventures well? Explain briefly. (2 points)







Model answer and marking guide






\(R^2=1-5272.57/9831.91\approx0.464\) (3 points). The fitted values explain 46.4% of the observed sample variation in sales-growth percentage points. It is not a percentage of correct predictions (3 points).
Adjusted \(R^2\) contains a penalty for every predictor in the model, and it can fall when a term adds little to the fit (2 points). It helps to compare models with different numbers of predictors that are fitted to the same outcome and the same observations (2 points).
\(H_0:\beta_{marketing}=\beta_{experience}=\beta_{team}=\beta_{digital}=0\) against the alternative that at least one of them is not zero (3 points). The p-value is far below 0.05, so reject \(H_0\): the model with four predictors fits better than a model with only an intercept, if the assumptions of the test hold (3 points).
The F-test is one joint test of all four coefficients together. Four separate t-tests answer four single questions. A set of terms can be jointly useful even when no single t-test rejects (2 points).
No. \(R^2\) measures the fit in this sample only. To judge predictions for future ventures, the model must be checked on new data that were not used to fit it (2 points).

title: Mock Exam: QM Intermediate
section: Question 4: Multiple regression and a dummy predictor (20 points)
text:
Question 4: Multiple regression and a dummy predictor (20 points)
The coefficient table below comes from lm(growth_pct ~ marketing_10k + experience_years + team_size + digital, data = ventures). The reference category for digital is No.
                  Estimate  Std. Error  t value  Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)          2.45       0.77       3.18     0.002
marketing_10k        1.34       0.10      13.40    <0.001
experience_years     0.26       0.04       6.23    <0.001
team_size            0.17       0.10       1.63     0.104
digitalYes           3.08       0.46       6.67    <0.001

Interpret marketing_10k, including the predictor step, outcome unit, held-fixed variables, and sample. (5 points)
Interpret digitalYes and name its reference category. (4 points)
Compare two otherwise identical ventures: A spends €20,000 on marketing, has 5 years of founder experience, a team of 4, and digital = No. B has the same values except it spends €40,000 and has digital = Yes. Calculate B’s fitted growth minus A’s. (5 points)
Test \(H_0:\beta_{team\_size}=0\) against a two-sided alternative and give a careful conclusion. (3 points)
Explain why including controls does not by itself give the marketing or digital coefficients a causal interpretation. (3 points)







Model answer and marking guide






Among sampled registry ventures, an additional €10,000 in annual marketing spending is associated with 1.34 percentage points higher fitted sales growth, holding founder experience, team size, and offering type fixed (5 points).
At equal marketing spending, experience, and team size, primarily digital ventures have fitted growth 3.08 percentage points higher than primarily physical ventures. No is the reference (4 points).
The spending change is two units, contributing \(2(1.34)=2.68\). Changing from No to Yes contributes 3.08. The fitted difference is \(2.68+3.08=5.76\) percentage points (5 points).
\(t=1.63\), \(p=0.104>0.05\), so do not reject \(H_0\). The data do not show an association between team size and growth, holding the other predictors fixed. This does not prove that the coefficient is zero (3 points).
Controls adjust only for variables that are measured and included in the model. Unmeasured confounders, reverse causality, selection, and measurement error can remain in these observational data (3 points).

title: Mock Exam: QM Intermediate
section: Question 5: Interactions, curvature, and a partial F-test (20 points)
text:
Question 5: Interactions, curvature, and a partial F-test (20 points)
The researcher fits the extended model
extended_model <- lm(
  growth_pct ~ spend_c * digital + I(spend_c^2) + experience_years,
  data = ventures
)
with estimates:
                         Estimate
(Intercept)                  9.20
spend_c                      1.04
digitalYes                   2.96
I(spend_c^2)                -0.11
experience_years             0.24
spend_c:digitalYes           0.68
The partial comparison with the additive linear model reports:
Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: growth_pct ~ spend_c + digital + experience_years
Model 2: growth_pct ~ spend_c * digital + I(spend_c^2) + experience_years
  Res.Df    RSS  Df  Sum of Sq    F   Pr(>F)
1    316  5317.0
2    314  5053.8   2     263.23  8.18  0.00035

At €40,000 of marketing spending (spend_c = 0), give the fitted spending slope for each offering type and the fitted Yes–No difference. (6 points)
At €60,000 (spend_c = 2), calculate the fitted Yes–No difference. (3 points)
For a physical-offering venture, calculate the fitted change when spending rises from €60,000 (spend_c = 2) to €70,000 (spend_c = 3), holding experience fixed. Repeat for a digital venture. (5 points)
State the hypotheses and conclusion of the partial F-test. (4 points)
State the hierarchy rule and one reason not to extrapolate this quadratic far beyond the observed spending range. (2 points)







Model answer and marking guide






At spend_c = 0, the physical-offering slope is 1.04 percentage points per €10,000 and the digital slope is \(1.04+0.68=1.72\) (2 points each). The fitted digital-minus-physical difference is 2.96 percentage points (2 points). The slopes 1.04 and 1.72 are the slopes of the two curves exactly at spend_c = 0. The fitted change from spend_c = 0 to spend_c = 1 is \(1.04-0.11=0.93\) for physical and \(0.93+0.68=1.61\) for digital offerings. Either pair earns the points if the reasoning is shown.
The group difference is \(2.96+0.68(2)=4.32\) percentage points (3 points).
For physical offerings, the change from 2 to 3 is \(1.04(1)-0.11(3^2-2^2)=1.04-0.55=0.49\) percentage points (2 points). For digital offerings, add the interaction change of 0.68, so the fitted change is 1.17 percentage points (2 points). Units and the held-fixed experience condition earn 1 point.
\(H_0:\beta_{spend\times digital}=\beta_{spend^2}=0\) against the alternative that at least one of the two is not zero (2 points). Since \(p=0.00035<0.05\), reject \(H_0\): the two added terms are jointly useful beyond the additive linear model, if the assumptions of the test hold (2 points).
Keep spend_c and digital in the model when their interaction or the square of spend_c is in it (1 point). A quadratic curve can turn sharply and give unrealistic values outside the observed range (1 point).




The points of the five questions sum to 100. Do the mock exam in R before you open the answers. Use the marking guide to check your calculations, and also your units, reference groups, statements about what is held fixed, uncertainty, and the limits of causal claims.

title: QM Advanced: Course overview
text:
Work in progress



QM Advanced takes place in the spring semester. Its chapters are being written and will appear here before the course starts.


QM Advanced builds on QM Intermediate and brings statistical modelling and research design together, in preparation for the quantitative thesis. The course ends with a written exam.

title: How to succeed in this course
text:
Minimum path and full path
Success in QM is not about talent for mathematics. It is about a short weekly routine that you repeat: prepare before class, take part in class, read and practise after class, and bring your attempts to the tutorial. Every lecture chapter is built around this routine. Every part of it has a stated time budget, so you always know what “enough” looks like.
Why this routine works:
The total time outside class is about 4 hours per week for QM Basic in weeks with two lectures (about the same in tutorial weeks), and about 1.5 to 2 hours per week for QM Intermediate (2.5 hours in the two tutorial weeks). Research on learning consistently finds that practice spread over the weeks works better than the same hours packed together before the exam.
Every chapter marks two paths through the work outside class.

text:
Working with AI, in one paragraph
Use Tilly and other AI tools under the standing protocol Attempt → Ask → Verify → Explain. Attempt the task yourself first and find where you are stuck. Ask for a hint or a diagnostic question, not for a full solution. Verify every answer against the data, the course notation, and the R output. Then explain the result in your own words. The exam tests what you can do with supplied output. The protocol makes AI sharpen that ability instead of replacing it.

Do not try to catch up by reading everything you missed. Go to the chapter of the most recent lecture. Read its lecture material once, answer its recall questions, and do its first practice task. title: R Refresher
text:
If regression commands are unfamiliar
Use the same object-first workflow throughout Intermediate:
model <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = my_data)
summary(model)
confint(model)
fitted(model)
residuals(model)
plot(model)

lm() fits the model specified to the right of ~ and uses the outcome on the left.
summary() reports coefficients, their classical tests, model fit, and the overall F-test.
confint() reports coefficient confidence intervals.
fitted() and residuals() return one value for each analysis row.
plot(model) opens the standard diagnostic plots.

Write the fitted object to a meaningful name and inspect the analysis sample before interpreting output. R silently omits rows containing missing values in variables used by lm() unless instructed otherwise. The Intermediate code sheet collects the full course workflow in one place.

sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv")
nrow(sharks)
mean(sharks$deal_on_show)
median(sharks$description_words)
table(sharks$season)
Then explain each output in words. If the code runs but you cannot explain the quantity, the remaining problem is statistical rather than programming.






Assessment reminder



Basic and Advanced end with written exams. In Basic you may be asked to verify, interpret, or describe supplied R code and output. Intermediate uses TestVision with live data work in R, so this refresher matters most for that course.

title: R Refresher
section: How the figures in this book are made
text:
How the figures in this book are made
Every data figure in this textbook carries its own R code: click “See the R code for this figure” above any graph to unfold it. Each code block is self-contained: copy it into a fresh R session in your course project and it reproduces the figure exactly. The exam never asks you to write ggplot2 code. The base R commands on the code sheet are enough there. Install the plotting packages once:
install.packages(c("ggplot2", "patchwork"))
The figures follow a small set of principles worth stealing for your own tutorials, reports, and thesis:

One message per graph. The caption states it. Everything that does not serve it is removed (no boxes, no minor gridlines, no decoration).
Counts start at zero, and there is only ever one vertical axis.
Colour is spent, not sprinkled. One colour carries the data (#009E73), a second marks contrast or a fitted line (#D55E00), grey holds context. Reference values (means, benchmarks, zero lines) are gold dashed lines with the value written next to them. The palette is colourblind-safe by construction.
Label directly where possible instead of forcing the reader through a legend, and always name axes with their units.
PMFs are drawn as stick-and-dot (lollipop) charts, histograms with stated bin widths, model curves as smooth lines with shaded probability areas.

If you want to go further, and for your thesis you will, three free references are the course’s recommended path: Wickham, Çetinkaya-Rundel & Grolemund, R for Data Science, Chapter 1 for ggplot2 itself, Healy, Data Visualization: A Practical Introduction for building good graphs in R end to end, and Wilke, Fundamentals of Data Visualization for the design principles behind every choice above.

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Numbers, proportions, percentages, and units
A proportion is a part divided by a total:
\[
\text{proportion}=\frac{\text{count in category}}{\text{total count}}.
\]
Convert a proportion to a percentage by multiplying by 100. A change from 40% to 46% is:

a 6 percentage-point increase
a \(6/40=15\%\) relative increase.

Keep units through every calculation. If \(Y\) is percentage-point equity and \(X\) is measured in seasons, a slope has units of percentage points per season. Rescaling dollars to thousands of dollars changes coefficient size but not the underlying fitted relationship.

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Order of operations
Use this order:

brackets or parentheses
powers and roots
multiplication and division
addition and subtraction.

For example,
\[
\frac{12-8}{\sqrt{16}}=\frac{4}{4}=1.
\]
In R:
(12 - 8) / sqrt(16)
Use parentheses generously in code when they make the intended calculation clear.

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Equality, approximation, and inequalities



Symbol
Read as




\(=\)
equals


\(\ne\)
does not equal


\(\approx\)
is approximately equal to


\(<,>\)
is less than, is greater than


\(\le,\ge\)
is less/greater than or equal to


\(\in\)
is an element of



Do not replace \(=\) with \(\approx\). A probability returned by rounded R output may be approximately 0.612. The fraction \(882/1441\) is exact for the file.
Interval notation:

\([a,b]\) includes both endpoints
\((a,b)\) excludes both endpoints
\((a,b]\) excludes \(a\) and includes \(b\).

For a continuous random variable, endpoint inclusion does not change a probability because individual points have probability zero.

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Variables, functions, and graphs
A variable is a symbol whose value may vary. A function assigns one output to each allowed input:
\[
y=f(x).
\]
In \(F_X(x)=P(X\le x)\), \(F_X\) names the CDF and \(x\) is the input at which it is evaluated. The subscript identifies the random variable whose distribution is described.
A graph’s horizontal axis displays the input or predictor. The vertical axis displays the function value or outcome. Read both labels and units before interpreting shape.

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Straight lines, slopes, and intercepts
A line is
\[
y=a+bx.
\]

\(a\) is the value of \(y\) at \(x=0\): the intercept.
\(b\) is the change in \(y\) for a one-unit increase in \(x\): the slope.

Between two points \((x_1,y_1)\) and \((x_2,y_2)\),
\[
b=\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}.
\]
The sign gives direction. The magnitude depends on both measurement units. An intercept need not be substantively meaningful when \(x=0\) is outside the observed range.

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Subscripts and indices
The symbol \(x_i\) means the value of variable \(x\) for observation \(i\). For \(n\) observations,
\[
x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n.
\]
In multiple regression, \(x_{ij}\) is the value of predictor \(j\) for observation \(i\). Keep the two roles separate:

\(i=1,\ldots,n\) indexes observations
\(j=1,\ldots,k\) indexes predictors.

Capital \(X_i\) usually denotes a random variable before sampling. Lower-case \(x_i\) denotes its observed value.

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Summation notation
The Greek letter sigma means “add”:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i=x_1+x_2+\cdots+x_n.
\]
The sample mean is
\[
\bar x=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i.
\]
For values 2, 5, and 8,
\[
\bar x=\frac{2+5+8}{3}=5.
\]
A weighted sum multiplies every value by its weight before adding. Expectation for a discrete random variable is a probability-weighted sum:
\[
E[X]=\sum_x x\,p_X(x).
\]

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Powers, roots, and squared deviations
The square is \(x^2=x\times x\). The square root reverses a non-negative square:
\[
\sqrt{x^2}=|x|.
\]
Squaring a deviation makes both signs positive and gives more influence to large deviations. This is why variance (Lecture 3) and least squares use squared terms.
If variance has squared units, its square root, the standard deviation, returns to the original units.
The square-root sample-size rule is central to standard errors:
\[
\operatorname{SE}(\bar X)=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.
\]
To halve the SE, multiply \(n\) by \(2^2=4\).

title: Mathematics Refresher
section: Degrees of freedom and t critical values
text:
Degrees of freedom and t critical values
Degrees of freedom count how many pieces of information remain free after estimating required quantities. For a one-sample t procedure, the \(n\) deviations from the sample mean satisfy
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i-\bar x)=0.
\]
After \(n-1\) deviations are known, the final deviation is fixed by this constraint. The procedure therefore uses
\[
df=n-1.
\]
The notation \(t_{0.975,df}\) means the value with 97.5% of a t distribution to its left. It leaves 2.5% in the right tail, so \(\pm t_{0.975,df}\) are the critical values for a 95% two-sided procedure. In R:
qt(0.975, df = 24)
With few degrees of freedom, the t distribution has heavier tails and the critical value is larger. It approaches the standard normal distribution as the degrees of freedom increase.
The same idea reappears in regression. If a model estimates an intercept and \(k\) slopes from \(n\) observations, the residual degrees of freedom are
\[
df=n-k-1.
\]

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Sets and event notation
A set is a collection of elements. In probability:

\(\Omega\) is the sample space
\(A\subseteq\Omega\) is an event
\(A^c\) is the complement, “not \(A\)”
\(A\cup B\) is the union, “\(A\) or \(B\), or both”
\(A\cap B\) is the intersection, “both \(A\) and \(B\)”
\(\varnothing\) is the empty event.

In conditional probability,
\[
P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)},
\]
the vertical bar means “given.” The event after the bar supplies the reference class and denominator.
Two events are independent when \(P(A\mid B)=P(A)\), or equivalently when \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)\,P(B)\). The product form is the algebraic check used in Lecture 4.

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Fractions and rearranging equations
Multiplying the numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number does not change a fraction. To solve a simple equation, apply the same operation to both sides.
Example:
\[
z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}
\]
implies
\[
z\sigma=x-\mu
\]
and therefore
\[
x=\mu+z\sigma.
\]
This rearrangement converts between a raw value and a z-score.

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Indicators and reference categories
An indicator takes values 0 and 1:
\[
D_i=
\begin{cases}
1,&\text{condition holds},\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
In \(Y=\beta_0+\beta_1D+\varepsilon\):

\(D=0\) gives mean \(\beta_0\)
\(D=1\) gives mean \(\beta_0+\beta_1\)
\(\beta_1\) is the 1-group minus 0-group difference.

For \(G\) categories and an intercept, use \(G-1\) indicators and name the omitted reference category.

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Products, interactions, and combined effects
An interaction contains a product \(XZ\):
\[
Y=\beta_0+\beta_1X+\beta_2Z+\beta_3XZ+\varepsilon.
\]
The slope of \(X\) is \(\beta_1+\beta_3Z\). When \(Z=0\), it is \(\beta_1\). When \(Z=1\), it is \(\beta_1+\beta_3\). Interpret the combined expression, not \(\beta_3\) alone.
Centering replaces \(X\) with
\[
X_c=X-\bar X.
\]
Then \(X_c=0\) represents the sample mean of \(X\), often making lower-order terms more meaningful. Centering changes coefficient representation but not the fitted values of a correctly re-expressed model.

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
Polynomial terms
A quadratic function is
\[
y=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2.
\]
Its one-unit change from \(x\) to \(x+1\) is
\[
\beta_1+\beta_2(2x+1),
\]
so there is no single constant slope. Evaluate fitted values at meaningful inputs and graph the curve within the observed range.
In an R formula, write a squared predictor as I(x^2) so R treats the expression arithmetically.

title: Mathematics Refresher
text:
References and further practice

OpenStax, College Algebra 2e provides free chapters on equations, functions, graphs, polynomials, and algebraic manipulation.
Khan Academy Algebra provides short explanations and practice on linear equations, functions, exponents, and polynomials.
R as a Calculator connects arithmetic and order of operations directly to R.

When practising with AI, ask for one problem at a time, show your working, and request feedback on the first incorrect step rather than a replacement answer.
